articles.title: RAG vs GraphRAG vs Knowledge Graphs: Choosing the Right Enterprise Knowledge Architecture
articles.description: Microsoft now reports sub-second retrieval with GraphRAG Zero. Yet independent benchmarks show...
articles.body_html:
Microsoft now reports sub-second retrieval with GraphRAG Zero. Yet independent benchmarks show graph-based systems can lose to ordinary RAG. RAG vs GraphRAG vs Knowledge Graphs isn't a race to add nodes. It's a decision about where your enterprise's answers actually live.

RAG vs GraphRAG vs Knowledge Graphs: The 60-Second Comparison

What Is the Difference Between RAG, GraphRAG, and Knowledge Graphs?

RAG retrieves relevant evidence, usually text passages, to ground an LLM's response. GraphRAG augments retrieval with relationships, graph neighborhoods, or graph-derived summaries to connect information across sources. A knowledge graph stores entities and explicit relationships as reusable enterprise data; applications can query it without generating text. RAG and GraphRAG are retrieval-grounded answering approaches. A knowledge graph is an information asset that either approach can use.

Decision Factor RAG GraphRAG Knowledge Graph
Primary purpose Find source passages Connect evidence across documents Represent verified relationships
Retrieval Keyword/vector search Graph traversal and graph-guided retrieval Graph queries and APIs
Best use cases FAQs, policies, documentation Multi-hop questions, cross-document analysis Dependencies, lineage, compliance
Main challenge Missing relevant context Graph quality and processing cost Entity resolution and maintenance
Output Grounded answers Connected insights and summaries Structured facts and relationship paths

Important: An automatically extracted GraphRAG index is not necessarily an authoritative enterprise knowledge graph.

Which Architecture Should Enterprises Choose?

The deciding factor is the question your application must answer.

Consider a procurement assistant connected to supplier contracts, purchase orders, incident reports, and operational data.

  • RAG: "What is Supplier A's termination notice period?" Retrieve the relevant contract clause.
  • Knowledge graph: "Which products depend on Supplier A through subcontractors?" Traverse verified supply relationships.
  • GraphRAG: "What recurring supplier risks emerged across this quarter's reports?" Connect evidence and synthesize patterns across documents.

When Is GraphRAG Worth the Extra Engineering?

GraphRAG is worth testing when answers require several connected documents, entity disambiguation, or a summary of patterns across a large collection. Graph traversal can bring related evidence together; community summaries can improve corpus-wide coverage. It is not automatically more accurate than hybrid RAG for one-document lookups. Benchmark actual enterprise questions because extraction errors, missing links, and maintenance costs can erase the benefit.

Microsoft's GraphRAG documentation describes local, global, and DRIFT search.

Its newer GraphRAG Zero research reports 0.93-second average context retrieval in a specific evaluation, not a universal production latency guarantee.

Meanwhile, AWS's September 2026 reference architecture combines GraphRAG and LightRAG on shared infrastructure, allowing developers to select retrieval methods per query.

The architectural shift is toward selective retrieval, not replacing every vector index with a graph.

When Should an Enterprise Build a Knowledge Graph?

Build a governed knowledge graph when relationships must remain consistent across multiple applications, not merely help one chatbot answer questions. Supplier dependencies, customer identities, ownership hierarchies, and data lineage often require stable identifiers, typed relationships, source provenance, and change history. Query those facts deterministically where possible; use RAG to explain them. A graph inferred solely from documents needs verification before it drives high-stakes decisions.

For example:

Supplier → supplies → Component → used_in → Product

Each relationship should have a source, owner, validity date, and access policy.

Building a Production-Ready Enterprise Knowledge Architecture

Start With Hybrid RAG, Then Add Graph Retrieval Selectively

A practical implementation should follow six stages:

  1. Data ingestion: Connect documents and business records with source identifiers, timestamps, and permissions.
  2. Hybrid search: Combine keyword and vector retrieval, followed by reranking.
  3. Entity resolution: Match business entities across documents and structured sources.
  4. Query routing: Select vector retrieval, graph traversal, or corpus-level synthesis.
  5. Answer generation: Return evidence-backed responses with source citations.
  6. Evaluation: Monitor correctness, latency, cost, and retrieval failures.

A simplified routing policy:

# Conceptual routing policy
def route(query):
    if needs_verified_relationships(query):
        return "knowledge_graph + source_documents"

    if needs_corpus_wide_synthesis(query):
        return "graphrag_global + source_documents"

    return "hybrid_rag + reranker"

The intent-detection functions require validation against real queries. This example illustrates routing logic, not a complete production implementation.

Security, Freshness, and Provenance Are Non-Negotiable

Enterprise retrieval must enforce:

  • Authorization: Apply access controls before retrieving or expanding graph relationships.
  • Provenance: Track source IDs and supporting evidence for important relationships.
  • Freshness: Propagate updates, deletions, and revoked permissions across indexes, graphs, and caches.
  • Validation: Keep deterministic calculations in SQL or governed business services.

Quokka Labs' eight-stage RAG retrieval failure ladder provides a practical framework for diagnosing chunking, retrieval ranking, and context assembly failures before introducing another architecture.

How Do You Benchmark RAG vs GraphRAG vs Knowledge Graphs?

Don't choose an architecture based on a vendor demonstration.

Build an evaluation set of 50 representative enterprise questions:

  • 20 single-document lookups
  • 20 multi-hop relationship questions
  • 10 corpus-wide synthesis questions

Use the same documents, model, and evaluation criteria across competing retrieval approaches.

Evaluation Metric What It Measures
Evidence recall Whether required sources were retrieved
Answer faithfulness Whether claims are supported by evidence
Relationship accuracy Correctness of entities, links, and dates
Security compliance Whether unauthorized evidence is excluded
P95 latency Response performance under load
Cost per answer Retrieval, indexing, and model expenses
Data freshness Delay between updates and searchable knowledge

Decision rule: Add graph complexity only when it improves relevant answer quality enough to justify additional engineering and operating costs.

This distinction matters. Independent GraphRAG-Bench research, published at ICLR 2026, reports that graph-based approaches frequently underperform standard RAG on certain real-world tasks.

For more implementation detail, explore Quokka Labs' Graph RAG vs Vector RAG comparison.

Real-World Experience: How Quokka Labs Approaches Enterprise Retrieval

At Quokka Labs, 15+ years of product engineering experience informs how we design AI-native applications around measurable workflows and governed data.

For Run The Day, Quokka Labs integrated a knowledge-connected AI assistant to help race directors access operational guidance and event information.

The implementation illustrates a practical principle: solve the document retrieval and workflow integration problem before introducing graph complexity.

The same discipline applies when adding entity relationships, agent workflows, or new knowledge sources.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is GraphRAG Better Than Traditional RAG?

Not universally. GraphRAG can provide stronger context for relationship-intensive or corpus-wide questions. Traditional or hybrid RAG can be more efficient for straightforward document retrieval.

Does GraphRAG Require a Knowledge Graph?

GraphRAG approaches generally use graph structure or graph-derived information. Some construct graphs from documents; others use existing knowledge graphs or lightweight graph representations.

Can Knowledge Graphs Eliminate LLM Hallucinations?

No. Knowledge graphs improve relationship traceability, but incorrect edges, stale data, and unsupported generation can still produce inaccurate answers.

Final Verdict: Choose the Architecture That Matches Your Evidence

RAG is a strong baseline for document-based enterprise AI. GraphRAG becomes valuable when connecting evidence across sources matters. Knowledge graphs are worth maintaining when verified business relationships must serve multiple systems.

The best architecture may combine all three but only where each contributes measurable value.

Need help making that decision?

For data protection, permission-aware retrieval, and AI governance, explore our trustworthy ai security services.

Your turn, DEV Community: What's the biggest limitation in your current RAG pipeline - document retrieval, multi-hop reasoning, or maintaining accurate enterprise relationships?

Share your experience in the comments. Let's compare what actually works in production.

articles.title: `npm config get` Knows Which Layer Won. It Just Won't Tell You.
articles.description: fluffydesk left a comment on my last piece about .npmrc layers, and it named the exact check I had...
articles.body_html:
fluffydesk left a comment on my last piece about .npmrc layers, and it named the exact check I had been skipping. I had shown that a repo's own .npmrc beats your user config: my user file says ignore-scripts=true, the repo says false, and the repo wins: the install hook runs. The check I recommended was npm config list, run inside the repo before installing, because it names the winning file.

fluffydesk asked about the check people actually run instead. npm config get ignore-scripts answers with the merged value from wherever you are standing: false inside the repo, true from home. Same command, two answers, and no mention that a vote happened. Worse, --location=user does not rescue it. The flag is accepted, and the command still returns false.

So I ran the comparison. Same setup as last time: user config true, project config false, a test package with an install hook that leaves a marker file when it runs. Thirteen commands, three locations, every answer recorded. The flag does nothing. That is the claim, and I know it sounds like a small thing, but a flag that is accepted and ignored is worse than a flag that errors, because it lets you walk away believing you asked one layer a question and got its answer.

Problem 1: the same command gives two answers, and neither says why

Inside the repo, npm config get ignore-scripts prints false. From home, the same command prints true. From the folder above the repo, true again. All three answers are the effective value for that spot, and all three are correct in the narrow sense. The install proves it: the hook ran in the repo and did not run in the clean folder. But none of them says which layer won. If you run the check from home and read true, you walk into the install believing hooks are off. They are not. The command answered the question you typed and hid the question you meant: who decided this?

That is the trap in its plainest form. The value is right and the understanding is wrong, and the understanding is the part that costs you.

Problem 2: --location=user is accepted, and then ignored

This is the one fluffydesk called, and they called it exactly. Inside the repo, npm config get ignore-scripts --location=user returns false. Not true, the user layer's value. false, the project-overridden value. The flag does not error, does not warn, does not print anything extra. It just takes your request to hear from the user layer and hands you the merged answer anyway.

I ran it from all three spots to be sure. Home: true. Run root: true. Inside the repo: false, with the flag on. The flag changes nothing about the value anywhere. If you believed --location=user was a way to interrogate one layer at a time, you were never interrogating anything. You were asking the same merged question with extra words attached.

A flag that errors is honest. A flag that is silently ignored is a trap with good manners.

Problem 3: --location=project outside a repo answers instead of refusing

The other direction is worse, because it invents an answer. From home, where no project config exists at all, npm config get ignore-scripts --location=project returns true, the user value, with no warning that there is no project layer to ask. From the run root, same thing: true, silence, no complaint.

Read that as a person would. You asked the project layer a question, and it answered. Except it did not. There is no project layer there. The command reached past the layer you named, took the next value down the chain, and handed it to you dressed as a project answer. If you are writing a check that runs in CI, in a directory you did not verify first, that silent fallback is the difference between "the repo has no override" and "I never actually looked at the repo".

Problem 4: only one command names the winner, and it is not the one with JSON

Plain npm config list, run from inside the repo, is the only command in the whole matrix that tells you which layer won. It prints the user value true stamped ; overridden by project, then names the winning file by its full path, ; "project" config from .../repo/.npmrc, and then the effective false. That stamp is the whole story in one line: a vote happened, here is who lost, here is the file that beat them.

npm config list --json shows "ignore-scripts": false and names no source file at all. So the machine-readable version is the one that drops the one fact you need, and the human-readable version is the one that keeps it. If your tooling parses the JSON, it gets the value and loses the provenance in the same breath.

And config list only tells the truth from inside the repo. From the parent folder, the project layer is invisible: true, user file named, no project section. Same command, same honesty, but the answer depends on where you stand, and standing in the wrong place is the easiest mistake in the whole chain.

Command Inside repo/ From home From outside Names the winner?
npm config get ignore-scripts false true true No
... --location=user false true true No
... --location=project false true true No
npm config list false true true Yes
npm config list --json false — — No

Every command took about 0.2 seconds. The check costs nothing. The wrong check costs a hook running on a machine you thought was protected.

Problem 5: the value was never wrong, which is why this keeps biting

Here is the part that keeps me from calling the whole thing broken. npm config get gets the effective value right every time. The install confirms it: hook ran in the repo at 00:14:01 UTC, no marker in the clean folder. If all you need is "what will the install do", get answers correctly from the right directory.

But "what will the install do" is not the question people are asking when they type get. They are asking "am I safe", and safety is a question about layers, not values. A true from home is not a promise about the repo. A false inside the repo is not an explanation of who set it. The command gives you the outcome and withholds the cause, and the cause is the thing you need when the outcome surprises you at 2 a.m. in a CI log.

So the rule I am keeping is narrow, and it is the same shape as the last piece: cd into the repo, then plain npm config list, not --json. Not because get lies. It does not. But because it answers the question you typed while the question you meant goes unasked. And if you ever catch yourself adding --location to make the answer more specific, stop. It is accepted, it changes nothing, and the silence afterwards is the command agreeing with a premise it never checked.

What check have you run that reported the loser without mentioning a vote happened? I would like to hear which command it was, and whether you found out from the output or from the hook running anyway.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: I Let AI Agents Rebrand My Entire OSS Ecosystem in One Night. Two Pipelines Were Silently Dead.
articles.description: Merged is a feeling. Live is a measurement. 13 PRs across 5 repos in one night of parallel AI agents — and two delivery pipelines that had been silently dead for weeks.
articles.body_html:
Two of my five repositories had delivery pipelines that were silently dead. Not failing loudly — dead. One site had served a two-week-old build while every deploy "ran". One repo had merged four PRs with zero CI checks since May.

I found out because of a rebrand. In one night, AI agents and I merged 13 pull requests across those five repos and repainted it from Tailwind violet to burnt orange. Nothing surfaces a dead pipeline like finally shipping something you care about seeing.

Merged is a feeling. Live is a measurement.

Pipeline one. The ESLint docs site had a deploy workflow that had failed on every run for two weeks. The rebrand merged — 1,580 tests green — and production kept serving the violet build from mid-July. Root cause: the workflow ran an unpinned npx vercel, drifted to a new major (58.4.4) whose bundled builder emits functions referencing files outside the build output directory. The deploy ships an archive of only that directory, so the platform side died with ENOENT on a file never packed. Dropping the archive flag is no escape hatch either — the artifact is 18,316 files against a 15,000-file deploy cap (measured on our plan, not quoted from docs). The fix was one line: pin every invocation to the CLI of the last green deploy — vercel@54.20.1, published 3 July and still what ran on the last deploy that worked, on 6 July. (58.4.4 published 30 July: an unpinned npx crossed four majors in under a month.)

# .github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml
env:
  VERCEL_CLI_VERSION: 54.20.1 # unpinned npx drifts majors; builder ENOENTs under --archive=tgz
# ...and every call has to actually consume it — the env var alone pins nothing:
#   npx vercel@${VERCEL_CLI_VERSION} build
#   npx vercel@${VERCEL_CLI_VERSION} deploy --prebuilt --archive=tgz

Pipeline two. The private repo that orchestrates all of this had its PR workflows manually disabled during a May billing crunch. Disabled workflows don't fail — they produce nothing. Four PRs merged over two months with an empty check rollup, which the merge button renders as invitingly as a passing one. The repair is one command per workflow; noticing took two months and a rebrand.

gh workflow list --all --json name,state   # state: disabled_manually

A green dashboard is a proxy metric for a working delivery pipeline, and like every proxy it fails in the direction that flatters you — the metric quietly becoming the target: a pipeline emitting nothing scores identically to one emitting success. Neither showed red. One showed stale green, the other silence — and silence renders as green if you don't look closely.

So here is the check I run now, and the one thing from that weekend I'd hand to someone else as-is:

The live check

A change is done when a request to production returns the thing you shipped — a version string, an asset hash, a hex value from the diff. Not when CI is green, not when the PR is merged, not when the deploy job reports success. Three failure modes it catches, in the order they bit me: built ≠ delivered (the deploy dies after the build passes), disabled ≠ passing (no checks renders like good checks), downstream ≠ upstream (the fix lands where the next sync overwrites it).

Why is a discipline doing a robot's job? It shouldn't be for long — the check is one curl of a version string away from being the deploy job's last step, failing the run when production disagrees with the artifact. Mine is still manual as I write this — exactly the admission the live check exists to force.

What the agents could not do

The agents wrote effectively all of the diff, each in an isolated worktree with its own PR and green checks. What they could not do was notice. Every one of those PRs was green. Neither dead pipeline was in any diff, so no reviewer — human or model — was going to find it by reading code.

That's the division of labor I build linters for AI-generated code around: the machine executes at a scale you can't, and the checks that face production are the part you own. Trust is not a feeling about the model. It's a property of the harness — and a harness that never queries production isn't one.

The ecosystem the agents rebranded is the Interlace ESLint plugins — source at github.com/ofri-peretz/eslint, packages at npmjs.com/~ofriperetz, and more of this at dev.to/ofri-peretz. Every number on those pages obeys the same-day-evidence rule as this article.

When did you last verify a pipeline delivered — not built, delivered? And what's the longest one stayed silently dead on you before something you shipped exposed it?

articles.title: Five trigger WHEN clauses Postgres will reject
articles.description: Postgres will reject some trigger WHEN clauses, but only when the migration runs.  A few rules that...
articles.body_html:
Postgres will reject some trigger WHEN clauses, but only when the migration runs.

A few rules that catch people out:

  1. A statement-level trigger can't read OLD or NEW in its WHEN. There's no single row to compare.
  2. An INSERT trigger can't read OLD. There is no old row.
  3. A DELETE trigger can't read NEW. There is no new row.
  4. An INSTEAD OF trigger on a view can't have a WHEN at all.
  5. A WHEN can't contain a subquery.

If you write triggers by hand in a custom migration, you find these out at deploy time.

In drizzle-pg-extras, my open-source package for declaring Postgres triggers, functions, comments and extensions next to a Drizzle schema, pgTrigger checks these when you declare the trigger, so generate fails before a bad migration is written:

export const touchUsers = pgTrigger("users_set_updated_at", {
  table: users,
  timing: "before",
  events: ["update"],
  columns: [users.email], // UPDATE OF
  when: ({ OLD, NEW }) => sql`${OLD.email} IS DISTINCT FROM ${NEW.email}`,
  function: setUpdatedAt,
});

It's a text scan, not a SQL parser, so Postgres still reports anything else when the migration runs. The README now spells out exactly what's checked and what isn't (0.6.1, on npm).

GitHub: https://github.com/Robertpaschal/drizzle-pg-extras
npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/drizzle-pg-extras

articles.title: I Built MLBox: A Browser Workbench That Shows How LLM Tokenizers Really Work
articles.description: Hi, I'm Mohit Verma, a Class 10 student from Patna, India, learning machine learning by building...
articles.body_html:
Hi, I'm Mohit Verma, a Class 10 student from Patna, India, learning machine learning by building things. MLBox is my open-source project: a browser workbench for LLM tokenizers, training intuition, and API pricing. Four tools, one static page, zero dependencies — every number is measured in your own browser.

Live demo: https://mohittt-vermaa.github.io/mlbox/
Code: https://github.com/mohittt-vermaa/mlbox

What's inside

Tokenizer lens — Paste any text and watch 7 real LLM tokenizers cut it up, token by token: counts, cost per million characters, a language cost matrix, a boundary diff between any two tokenizers, and a shareable link that freezes the whole comparison.

Micro playground — A neural net with hand-written backprop training live on canvas. Watch gradient descent solve XOR.

No-GPU recipes — 12 curated ML projects that genuinely finish on a laptop or a free Colab session, each with its one gotcha spelled out.

LLM price bench — 13 current models from 5 providers, transcribed from each provider's own pricing page with source links, plus a workload calculator and a real-prompt cost estimator.

The number that motivated all of this

Paste "नमस्ते दुनिया" ("hello world" in Hindi, 13 characters) and the tokenizers disagree: GPT-4o's tokenizer needs 5 tokens, Llama 3.1 needs 9, GPT-3.5/4's cl100k needs 13. Same two words, nearly 3x the bill depending on which tokenizer sits in front. Token choice is a cost multiplier and a context-window multiplier, and almost nobody looks at it.

Verified, not approximate

The tokenizer engine re-implements both BPE families in about 550 lines of dependency-free JavaScript, and the test suite checks it token-for-token against the upstream Rust implementations: 218,877 tokens, exact match on all seven models. There is also an Android app and a Windows desktop build in the releases, and everything runs offline with no API key and no backend — your text never leaves your machine.

Why I built it

I kept reading claims about token costs from blog posts instead of measuring them. MLBox is my way of learning ML properly: build the tool, verify every number, and share it so the next student can measure things themselves.

If it helps you, a star on GitHub means a lot: https://github.com/mohittt-vermaa/mlbox

— Mohit Verma
All my work: https://mohittt-vermaa.github.io

articles.title: How to Embed a Booking System Into Your Website or App (2026)
articles.description: Four real ways to embed booking into an existing site or web app: hosted link, iframe, vendor widget, or a booking API, with code and what breaks each.
articles.body_html:
"Can we add booking to the site?" is one of those requests that sounds like a script tag and turns into a sprint. Sometimes it genuinely is a script tag. Sometimes the script tag is the thing that makes the project fail six weeks later, when the client asks why the calendar looks nothing like the rest of the site and why Safari users keep losing their basket.

There are four real ways to put booking inside an existing website or web app, and they're not points on a single scale — they trade different things away. This is a walk through all four with the code, plus the failure modes I've watched teams hit with each one. I build Opencals, a booking API and platform, so the API section uses it; the first three approaches are vendor-agnostic and the caveats apply whichever tool you're embedding.

Key takeaway: Pick the embed approach by what has to match your brand and what has to survive a browser update. Linking out is the most reliable and the least yours. An iframe is fast but constrained by the vendor's CSP and by third-party cookie rules. A vendor widget looks native until you need it to behave differently. Building on a booking API costs the most upfront and is the only option that gives you full control of the UI and the data.

The four approaches at a glance

Approach Time to ship Design control Main risk
Link out to a hosted booking page An hour None beyond vendor theming Customers leave your site mid-funnel
Iframe the hosted page A day Low Vendor CSP, iframe height, third-party cookies
Vendor JavaScript widget A day or two Medium You inherit the vendor's UX and bundle
Build on a booking API / SDK One to three weeks Total You own the frontend forever

Two thirds of the projects I see should use approach 1 or 2 and don't, because "embedded" sounds more professional than "link". The other third try approach 2 for something that genuinely needed approach 4, and spend the difference in workarounds.

Approach 1 — link out to a hosted booking page

The vendor hosts the booking flow on their domain or a subdomain of yours. You link to it. That's the whole integration.

<a
  href="https://book.example.com/services/beard-trim?staff=marek"
  class="btn btn-primary"
>
  Book an appointment
</a>

Most hosted booking pages accept query parameters to preselect a service, a staff member, a location, or a date. Use them. A link that lands on a generic service list converts noticeably worse than one that lands on the specific service the customer was just reading about — you already know what they clicked, so pass it along.

If the vendor supports a return URL, set it, so a completed booking sends the customer back to a page you control and you can fire your own conversion event there.

Pros

  • Nothing to maintain — the vendor ships fixes, you get them
  • No CSP, cookie, or iframe-height problems at all
  • Works identically on every browser and every screen size
  • Deep links let you preselect service, staff, and location

Cons

  • The customer leaves your domain in the middle of the funnel
  • Branding is limited to whatever theming the vendor exposes
  • Analytics needs cross-domain setup or you lose attribution
  • The booking page is rented — it isn't on your domain and doesn't leave with you

For a marketing site whose job is to get someone to book, this is very often the correct answer, and the "unprofessional" objection is mostly imaginary. Customers hand their card details to Stripe-hosted checkouts on a different domain every day.

Approach 2 — iframe the hosted page

An iframe keeps the customer on your page while the vendor renders the flow. It's a genuine middle ground, and it has three specific traps.

<div class="booking-frame">
  <iframe
    src="https://yourshop.opencals.com/book"
    title="Book an appointment"
    loading="lazy"
    allow="payment"
  ></iframe>
</div>

<style>
  .booking-frame {
    position: relative;
    width: 100%;
    min-height: 720px;
  }
  .booking-frame iframe {
    position: absolute;
    inset: 0;
    width: 100%;
    height: 100%;
    border: 0;
  }
</style>

Trap one: the vendor's CSP decides whether this works at all. Any booking page worth using sets a frame-ancestors directive so it can't be silently framed by a phishing site. If your domain isn't in that list, your iframe renders a blank box and a console error, and no amount of CSS fixes it. The Opencals storefront works this way — framing is allowlisted per domain rather than open by default, so you ask for your domain to be added before you build against it. Check this on day one with any vendor, not after the layout is done.

Trap two: height. A booking flow changes height as the customer moves from service list to calendar to checkout. A fixed-height iframe either clips the checkout or leaves 400px of dead space on the service list. The clean fix is postMessage — if the vendor emits resize events, listen for them:

window.addEventListener("message", (event) => {
  if (event.origin !== "https://yourshop.opencals.com") return;
  if (event.data?.type !== "resize") return;
  document.querySelector(".booking-frame").style.minHeight =
    `${event.data.height}px`;
});

Always check event.origin. A message listener that trusts any sender is a real vulnerability, not a lint warning. If the vendor doesn't emit resize events, set a generous min-height and accept the whitespace — polling scrollHeight across origins is not possible, and the hacks that claim otherwise don't work anymore.

Trap three: third-party context. Inside an iframe, the vendor's cookies are third-party cookies. Safari's tracking prevention has blocked those for years, and Chrome's rules keep tightening. Vendors that depend on a session cookie to hold a basket across steps can drop bookings in the middle of checkout, and it reproduces only in the browsers you don't develop in. Test a full booking in Safari on an actual iPhone before you ship. Not the simulator, and not desktop Safari with default settings.

Test the iframe in Safari, on a phone, in a private window. Every iframe embed bug report I've seen started with "it works fine on my machine". Third-party storage restrictions, mobile keyboards resizing the viewport, and date pickers that expect the full screen all show up on a real phone and nowhere else. Ten minutes of testing here saves a support thread that runs for a month.

Approach 3 — a vendor JavaScript widget

A widget is a script the vendor gives you that mounts their UI into a container in your page. Calendly, Acuity and most appointment tools ship one; the typical shape is a container plus an init call.

<div id="booking"></div>
<script src="https://vendor.example.com/widget.js" defer></script>
<script>
  window.addEventListener("load", () => {
    VendorBooking.mount("#booking", {
      shop: "yourshop",
      service: "beard-trim",
      theme: "light",
    });
  });
</script>

Under the hood, most widgets are still an iframe — they just manage its height and lifecycle for you, which removes trap two above but not traps one and three. Some render directly into your DOM, which is better for styling and worse for isolation: their CSS reset and yours will disagree about something eventually.

The real cost of a widget is that you inherit the vendor's product decisions. If their flow asks for a phone number and your client insists it's optional, you can't change it. If they load 180KB of JavaScript on a page that had a 40KB budget, that's now your Lighthouse score.

Worth being straight about this one: Opencals doesn't ship a universal drop-in script for arbitrary websites today. The widget exists inside the Shopify integration, where it installs as a theme block and inherits your Shopify theme. Everywhere else, the supported paths are the hosted storefront (approaches 1 and 2, with design customization for colours, fonts and logo) or the API. If a one-line script for any website is your hard requirement, a vendor that ships one is the better fit and I'd rather say so than sell you a workaround.

Approach 4 — build the flow on a booking API

The last option isn't embedding someone else's UI at all. You call a booking API for availability, cart, and payment, and you write the frontend yourself. Everything the customer sees is your code, on your domain, in your component library.

This is the headless approach, and it's the right call when the booking flow is part of the product rather than a page on a brochure site — when it needs your auth, your design system, or your own multi-step logic.

With Opencals, install the typed SDK and keep the key server-side:

npm i @opencals/storefront-sdk

// lib/opencals.ts — import it from server code only
import { setupOpencals } from "@opencals/storefront-sdk";
import { nextBuyerIp } from "@opencals/storefront-sdk/next";

setupOpencals({
  apiKey: process.env.OPENCALS_API_KEY!, // private key, spk_...
  buyerIp: nextBuyerIp, // forwards each visitor's IP, so rate limits count per visitor
  throwOnError: true,
});

Then the core of the flow is three steps: list what's bookable, ask for real availability, hold the slot in a cart.

import "@/lib/opencals";
import { AppointmentService, CartService, ProductService } from "@opencals/storefront-sdk";

// 1. What can be booked
const { data: page } = await ProductService.list({ query: { status: ["active"] } });
const service = page.data[0];

// 2. When is it actually free — computed from staff hours,
//    existing bookings, service duration and buffers (one day per call)
const { data: slots } = await ProductService.getCurrentAvailabilities({
  path: { productId: service.id },
  query: { date: "2026-08-18", timezone: "Europe/Warsaw" },
});

// 3. Hold the chosen slot in a cart (times are UTC)
const { data: cart } = await CartService.createOrGet({ headers: { "X-Cart-Id": "" } });
const { productId, fromDate, fromTime, toDate, toTime } = slots[0];
await AppointmentService.create({
  body: {
    slot: { productId, fromDate, fromTime, toDate, toTime },
    numberOfAttendees: 1,
    cartId: cart.id,
  },
});

Checkout is two more calls: CheckoutService.start returns a Stripe client secret for a Payment Element (no Stripe key in your app), and CheckoutService.submit places the order once the browser has confirmed the payment. These match @opencals/storefront-sdk 0.3.20 (checked November 2026).

A private storefront key can create real bookings and take payments, so it belongs in a Route Handler, a Server Action, or your own backend — never in a client bundle. Same rule as a Stripe secret key.

The availability call is the one that justifies the whole approach. Computing which slots are genuinely open means resolving staff schedules, service durations, buffers, existing bookings, group capacity and location hours together, and getting it race-safe so two customers can't hold the same slot. That's the part teams underestimate when they decide to build booking from scratch, and the part you're buying when you call an API instead.

For a complete walkthrough with the cart, checkout and confirmation screens wired up, see adding booking to a Next.js app with a REST API. The booking SDK reference covers the typed methods, and the booking API guide covers what to look for in any scheduling API, not just this one.

Pros

  • Complete control of the UI, the copy, and the number of steps
  • Booking lives on your domain, inside your auth and your analytics
  • One integration can serve web, mobile, and a Shopify store
  • No iframe, no third-party cookies, no CSP negotiation

Cons

  • One to three weeks of frontend work, not an afternoon
  • You own every bug in the booking UI from then on
  • Overkill for a brochure site whose only goal is a booked slot
  • Needs a developer available for changes the client used to self-serve

How to choose

  1. Does the booking flow need your auth or your data? If a logged-in customer should see their own history, pricing, or credits, an embedded vendor flow can't know who they are. Go to the API approach.
  2. Does the design have to be exactly yours? Not 'on-brand' — exactly yours, down to spacing and typography. If a themable vendor UI is acceptable, stop at the hosted page or a widget and save two weeks.
  3. Who maintains it in a year? If the client changes their own services and hours and has no developer, a hosted page they can configure themselves beats a custom frontend that needs a ticket for every change.
  4. Check the vendor's frame-ancestors policy before designing Framing an external booking page is only possible if the vendor allowlists your domain. Ask first — it decides whether approach 2 is on the table at all.
  5. Test the whole flow on a real phone in Safari Third-party storage, viewport resize on keyboard open, and native date pickers behave differently there. This is where embedded flows actually fail.
  6. Decide where the conversion event fires Whatever you choose, make sure a completed booking lands somewhere your analytics can see it, whether that's a return URL, a postMessage event, or your own confirmation route.

Where Opencals fits

Opencals is a booking and service-commerce platform with a public Storefront API, so it covers approaches 1, 2 and 4 directly, and approach 3 only inside Shopify.

If you want the fastest path: a hosted storefront on yourshop.opencals.com, styled with your colours, fonts and logo, linked from the pages where customers decide to book. If you want it framed inside your own page, that works once your domain is allowlisted. If you're an agency or a product team that needs the booking UI to be genuinely yours, the Storefront API and SDK give you the availability engine, cart, payments and post-booking management, and you build the rest — the MIT-licensed Next.js templates are a working starting point rather than a demo.

Pricing (opencals.com/pricing, checked November 2026) is $0.99 per appointment on the Elastic plan with no monthly fee, or a fixed plan from $14.98 a month with 300 appointments included (up to 3 locations and 10 staff self-serve). There's no per-seat charge on either, which matters if you're an agency running this for several clients rather than one business. Building and testing in a development store is free.

Frequently asked questions

Can I embed a booking system without an iframe?

Yes, in two ways. Some vendors ship a JavaScript widget that renders directly into your DOM, and any booking platform with a public API lets you build the UI yourself and call the API from your own frontend. The API route avoids every iframe constraint — CSP, height, third-party cookies — at the cost of building and maintaining the booking screens.

Why is my booking iframe blank?

Almost always the vendor's Content-Security-Policy. Booking pages set a frame-ancestors directive so they can't be framed by arbitrary sites, and if your domain isn't listed the browser refuses to render the frame and logs a CSP error in the console. Check the console first, then ask the vendor to allowlist your domain. A blank iframe is rarely a CSS problem.

Do embedded booking widgets hurt page speed?

They can. A typical widget loads its own JavaScript, fonts, and often an iframe document, which is easily 150–300KB before anything renders. Load it lazily, mount it below the fold or behind a button, and measure with Lighthouse before and after. If the widget sits above the fold on your highest-traffic page, a link to a hosted page is usually faster and converts about the same.

Can I preselect a service or staff member in an embedded booking flow?

Usually yes, via query parameters on the hosted URL or options passed to the widget's init call — service, staff, location and date are the common ones. It is worth wiring up: sending someone to a generic service list when you already know what they clicked adds a step that loses bookings.

Is it better to embed booking or build it with an API?

Embed when the booking flow is a page on a marketing site and a themed vendor UI is acceptable — it ships in a day and the vendor maintains it. Build on an API when booking is part of your product, needs your authentication, or has to match a design system exactly. The deciding question is whether you'll still want to change how the flow behaves in six months.

How do I track conversions from an embedded booking flow?

Decide up front where the completed-booking event fires. With a hosted page, set a return URL to a confirmation route on your own domain and fire the event there. With an iframe or widget, listen for the vendor's completion postMessage and validate event.origin before acting on it. With an API build, you already control the confirmation route, so it is just a normal event.

Related reading

  • Add booking to a Next.js app: The full API build, with cart and checkout code you can copy.
  • What is a headless booking system?: When the API approach is worth the extra weeks — and when it isn't.
  • How to build a booking website: The three approaches compared: SaaS, Shopify app, and headless API.
  • Opencals for developers: Storefront API, typed TypeScript SDK, and open templates.

The short version

If the booking flow is a page on a marketing site, link to a hosted booking page and spend the saved time on the copy around it. If it has to stay visually inside your page and the vendor allowlists your domain, iframe it — and test it on a phone in Safari before you call it done. If booking is part of your product, build it on an API and accept that you now own the frontend.

The mistake worth avoiding is choosing approach 2 for a job that needed approach 4, then spending three weeks fighting postMessage and cookie policies to get 60% of what a proper API build would have given you in the same time. If you're not sure which side of that line you're on, get in touch — it's usually a ten-minute conversation.

articles.title: My tests were green. They caught 0 of 10 real bugs.
articles.description: I had a small web shop with four end-to-end tests. All four passed, every time. I felt good about...
articles.body_html:
I had a small web shop with four end-to-end tests. All four passed, every time. I felt good about them.

Then I broke the shop on purpose, ten different ways, and ran the same four tests against each broken version. They caught zero.

That's the problem I built Saboteur to measure: a green suite tells you nothing about what it misses. I built it for the KaneCLI Online Hackathon by TestMu AI.

Live report: https://softalpha0.github.io/saboteur/
Code: https://github.com/softalpha0/saboteur

The idea in one paragraph

Saboteur plants one small, realistic bug at a time, builds the app, and runs your test suite against it. If every test still passes, the bug "slipped". For each bug that slipped, Claude writes a new test, and the test is only kept if it passes on the correct app and fails on the bugged one. No test gets in on the model's word alone.

This is basically mutation testing, but for end-to-end browser tests instead of unit tests, with an AI closing the gaps and a real browser acting as the judge.

The pieces

The tests are Kane CLI _test.md files: plain English steps that Kane runs in a real Chrome browser. Here is one of the four starter tests:

---
mode: testing
url: http://localhost:4173
tags: [starter, cart]
max_steps: 30
---

# Cart shows the added item

## Add the mug
Open the home page and add the Ceramic Mug to the cart.
Verify the cart badge in the header shows 1.

## Open the cart
Open the cart page.
Verify a line item named "Ceramic Mug" is listed with a unit price of $14.50.

The bugs are git patches. Each one is the kind of mistake that ships for real. This one makes the "+" quantity button do nothing:

-        onClick={() => onChange(value + 1)}
+        onClick={() => onChange(value)}

The ten bugs in the demo shop include a cart total that skips the last item, a discount code that takes 1% instead of 10%, a checkout that accepts the email a@, and a cart that empties when you refresh.

The loop for each bug:

  1. Copy the app to a temp folder, git apply the patch, build it, serve it.
  2. Run the whole suite with Kane CLI, with self-healing off (--no-adaptive-heal). With healing on, Kane would try to work around a broken page, which is great for flaky selectors and terrible for catching bugs.
  3. Score it: caught or slipped.

Being strict about what counts as "caught"

This took most of the work, and it's the part I'd tell anyone building something similar to care about most.

A failed test is not the same as a caught bug. While building this I saw tests fail because:

  • Chrome crashed (browser_disconnected)
  • my disk filled up mid-run and Chrome couldn't write screenshots
  • Kane's own page check errored (analyzer_failed)
  • a hover simply didn't land the first time

If you count those as catches, your score is a lie. So Saboteur:

  • treats crashes, disk errors and Kane-side errors as errors, never catches, and retries them
  • re-runs every catch on its own. If the test doesn't fail a second time, the first failure is treated as flaky and the whole suite runs again

That second rule saved me on a real run. On two bugs, a test failed with analyzer_failed, which had nothing to do with the bug. The confirm run passed, the suite re-ran clean, and both bugs were correctly scored as slipped instead of fake catches.

Closing the gaps with Claude

For every bug that slipped, Claude gets the bug's description, the app's routes and facts, and the existing tests, and writes a new _test.md. Then Kane runs it twice:

Run Build Healing Must
A correct app on pass
B bugged app off fail

If run A fails, the test is wrong about the app. If run B passes, the test doesn't catch the bug. Either way, Kane's failure text goes back to Claude for another try, up to three attempts. Only tests that pass both checks join the suite.

Results (all from real Kane runs)

Demo shop: the 4 starter tests caught 0 of 10 bugs. With Claude's Kane-proven tests: 10 of 10.

Duel mode. I then pointed two Claude agents at each other. Red reads the current tests and invents new bugs they would miss. Blue writes tests to catch them. Kane referees, and a bug only counts if Kane can see it in the browser (the check passes on the bugged app and fails on the correct one).

Final score: Red 3, Blue 3. Red found three real holes:

  • the cart badge counted products instead of items
  • free shipping was checked before the discount was applied
  • signing out left you signed in

Blue closed all three, and the suite grew from 18 to 21 tests.

An app I didn't write. A demo app I built myself is easy to game, so I also ran it on the official React TodoMVC with ten new bugs. Four typical starter tests (add, complete, delete, edit a todo) caught 2 of 10. Claude has written Kane-proven tests for 6 of the 8 misses so far. The final two were cut short when Kane lost its sign-in mid-run.

Things that went wrong

  • The first full attack took hours. Every bug is a fresh build plus a full browser run. Running two tests at a time, stopping at the first failure on attacks, and saving progress so an interrupted run can resume brought a caught bug down to a few minutes.
  • A Kane run hung for over two hours. On Windows, kane-cli runs behind a cmd launcher, so my timeout killed the launcher and left the real process alive. The fix was killing the whole process tree, plus a watchdog that stops a run when no output arrives for ten minutes.
  • A full disk looks like flaky tests. Kane keeps screenshots for every run. When my disk hit zero, tests started failing in odd ways. Saboteur's doctor command now checks free space before it starts.
  • Claude got every test right on the first attempt in my real runs, so the "send Kane's failure back to Claude" loop has never had to fire for real. It's covered by automated tests, but I want to see it in a live run.

Try it 

git clone https://github.com/softalpha0/saboteur
cd saboteur
pnpm i
kane-cli login
pnpm saboteur doctor --replay
pnpm saboteur run --replay

--replay needs no Claude key. It uses the tests Claude already wrote and Kane already proved. To point it at your own app, edit saboteur.config.json (build command, serve command, URL) and add your own bug patches.

The question I keep coming back to: how many of your tests would still pass if the feature they test was broken? I'd love to hear what you find if you try it.

articles.title: Browser Autofill Testing: Follow the Filled Form Into the Saved SaaS Record
articles.description: Browser autofill testing should follow the values all the way into the saved product record. Start...
articles.body_html:
Browser autofill testing should follow the values all the way into the saved product record. Start with safe test details, choose a browser suggestion, inspect every field it fills, correct one value, submit the form, and reopen the result. A form that looks complete may still behave differently from one filled by typing.

For a founder building in public, that is a useful peer-testing request. It gives another developer a specific task to try in a known environment. The public update can show the observed mismatch and recovery without exposing the tester's real address, contact list or browser profile.

Define the record the form is meant to create

Use a fictional SaaS contact manager as an example. Its new-contact form asks for a person's name, organization, email and postal address. The intended result is one contact record containing the reviewed values. Creating the record must not send an invitation or start a sales email in this exercise.

Prepare a disposable test workspace and confirm those boundaries before asking a peer to participate. If saving a contact normally triggers messages, provide a safe test route that suppresses delivery. A public request to “try our form” is too vague when the button can affect somebody outside the test.

Write down what the saved record should contain. In this example, the organization needs to be the contact's current company, which may differ from an older organization in an autofill profile. That difference gives the tester a reason to inspect and correct the suggestion rather than accept it automatically.

Use synthetic data and describe the browser conditions

Give the peer invented details that cannot be confused with a real customer. Use an address reserved for documentation where an email field is required, and keep outbound delivery disabled. Do not ask them to display their personal suggestion menu in a public recording.

Chrome's Autofill panel documentation describes inspecting address-field mappings and using provided test address data. That panel covers address information; it is not a complete test of every password manager, browser or input method.

Record the browser version, operating system and whether a browser feature or an extension supplied the values. Note whether the profile began with stored test data or used an offered test address. These conditions help another developer reproduce the observation without needing the original person's private setup.

A clean profile is useful for a repeatable case, but it is only one case. A returning user's older saved details may create different suggestions. Keep that as a separate follow-up with synthetic data, rather than quietly changing the conditions halfway through the first test.

Inspect the filled fields before touching them

Open the blank form and choose one available test suggestion. Observe which fields change. Read the displayed values, the required-field messages and the submit button's state. Avoid clicking through every field immediately, because that may trigger behavior that did not occur when autofill populated it.

The HTML autocomplete attribute gives browsers guidance about expected field values. MDN distinguishes values such as name, organization and email. Appropriate hints are a useful implementation check, but their presence does not prove that the whole product workflow works.

In the fictional case, suppose the name and email appear, while the form still says an email is required. Capture the visible contradiction. Then check whether focusing and leaving the email field changes the message. That sequence distinguishes the initial autofill result from a later interaction that may have caused the product to notice it.

Do not turn the workaround into the expected behavior. Requiring a person to touch an already filled field is a finding to investigate, even if it lets the test continue.

Correct one suggestion and follow the correction

Change the fictional organization's old name to the intended current name. Leave the other fields alone. Check whether the form recognizes the correction, whether any dependent summary updates, and whether a later browser suggestion unexpectedly replaces the edited value.

Next, submit once. Read the confirmation and reopen the contact through the normal product interface. Compare the displayed name, organization, email and address with the values reviewed just before submission. The result you need is the product's saved record, not the browser's memory of what it filled.

If the correction is missing, record exactly where the value changed. Was the old organization still visible before submission? Did the confirmation display the new one while the reopened record showed the old one? Different sequences point to different places for investigation.

This is where a developer's diagnostic work begins. The peer's report should preserve the observed sequence without guessing which event handler or state library caused it. A specific reproduction is more useful than a confident implementation theory attached to an incomplete screenshot.

Add a typed comparison and a recovery case

Reset the workspace, then create another synthetic contact by typing the same kind of values. Compare the field messages, button state and reopened record. Keep the input method as the main difference so the contrast remains interpretable.

If typing works and autofill does not, you have a narrower reproduction. You have not proved that all browser filling is broken. If both fail, the defect may belong to the broader form or save flow. Describe that result without forcing it into the original hypothesis.

Then test one relevant recovery. For example, leave a required field missing, submit, and use autofill or a manual correction to supply it. Check that the earlier error clears when the form accepts the value and that the final saved record is correct.

Avoid expanding the session into every possible form test. Keyboard order, duplicate submissions and network failure deserve their own checks. You can list those as untested boundaries while keeping this request focused on automatic filling, correction and persistence.

Give a peer a small test brief they can finish

A practical invitation names the test URL, disposable account, synthetic data, environment to record and expected saved result. State that no real customer information is needed. Explain where to report a mismatch and when to stop if the workflow leaves the safe test environment.

On Buildside, the founder community I founded, a public progress update can explain why you are checking this path and invite relevant developer feedback. Do not assume a general founder audience uses the browser combination you need. Ask for that condition explicitly, while making clear that participation is optional.

Keep private access details out of the public update. You can describe the task publicly and arrange approved test access separately. A usable invitation should let someone judge whether they can help without asking them to reveal their own stored information.

Thank the peer with a concrete resolution when the finding is addressed. Give them the revised test conditions and ask whether they want to recheck. A fresh test is more informative than assuming a code change removed the observed problem.

Publish the result at the level you actually checked

An honest update might say that an autofilled test email remained flagged as missing in one browser, and the revised form now saves the reviewed contact in that same reproduced case. Include the tested version and the remaining browser combinations you have not checked.

Show synthetic before-and-after values if they help explain the correction. Keep the browser suggestion menu out of the public image unless every visible detail is safe. Preserve meaningful field labels so another developer can understand what changed.

Autofill success is a sequence: a suggestion reaches the right fields, the user can inspect and correct it, validation reflects the current values, and the saved record contains the reviewed details. Building in public makes that sequence available for useful peer review. A full-looking form is only the beginning of the evidence.

articles.title: Recreating Minecraft's XP bar with three SVGs and one @keyframes rule
articles.description: On the Agoralis player dashboard, the job progress box shows a green XP bar that shimmers exactly...
articles.body_html:
On the Agoralis player dashboard, the job progress box shows a green XP bar that shimmers exactly like the one above the hotbar in Minecraft. Players recognise it instantly, and it shows their real job XP, pulled from the game server.

There is no canvas, no JavaScript and no GIF behind it. It is three small SVGs drawn pixel by pixel, one @keyframes rule that swaps two of them, and a Blade loop that decides how many segments to draw. This article shows the production code, why we picked this approach, and the edge cases we know it has.

TL;DR

  • Draw the bar as pixel-art SVGs: one tile for the empty track, two frames for a filled segment. Our second frame is the first one rotated 180°.
  • Tile the empty track with background-repeat: repeat-x and stack filled segments as 20 × 8 px flex children on top of it.
  • Alternate the two frames with a @keyframes rule on the background. We set the duration (0.7 s) by watching the game side by side.
  • Compute the number of filled segments server-side from the player's real values (currentXp / jobXp), so the bar is plain HTML that Livewire re-renders.
  • Guard the edges: zero XP, a zero divisor, rounding and prefers-reduced-motion.

The context

Agoralis is an economic role-play Minecraft server. The game itself is written in Java by the server team; we built everything that runs in the browser: the site, the player web app and the Filament admin, on Laravel and Livewire. The web app talks to the game server over RCON. The full project story (timeline, constraints, team) is here.

One screen shows the player's current job: level, skills, and how much XP is left before the next level. The server team wanted it to look like the game. The XP bar is the element every Minecraft player knows, so we wanted it close to pixel-perfect, including the subtle shimmer of the filled part.

The constraints were plain. We were a team of two on the whole web app, the game server was still being built in parallel, and many players use the dashboard on a phone while the game runs on their main screen. A decorative bar had to cost almost nothing to build, to run and to maintain.

Option What it costs Why we didn't keep it
CSS gradient + width transition Cheap Looks like a generic progress bar, not like Minecraft's pixels
Canvas or JS animation A render loop, resize handling, more code to test Too much machinery for a decorative element
Animated GIF/APNG of the full bar One file Cannot reflect the player's real value without one image per percentage
Pixel-drawn SVG frames + @keyframes Three small files, about 15 lines of CSS Kept: same look as the game, dynamic width, no JS

The design came first: our designer reproduced the bar pixel by pixel in the mockup, already knowing it would be built as frames swapped by CSS rather than as a real animation.

Drawing the frames at pixel level

The bar is made of three SVG files, each one a grid of 1-pixel rectangles exported from the mockup.

File Size Role
xpEmpty.svg 26 × 8 px Empty track tile, repeated horizontally
xpFull.svg 20 × 6 px Filled segment, frame A
xpFull2.svg 20 × 6 px Filled segment, frame B

Each pixel is one <path> with its own fill. The highlights (#8CF139) sit in the middle rows and the shadows (#3F7F07) at the edges, which is what gives the bar its relief. The last 2 px column is a dark separator, like the notches in the game's bar.

<!-- xpFull.svg (excerpt): 18 × 6 coloured pixels + a 2 px dark separator -->
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="20" height="6" viewBox="0 0 20 6" fill="none">
    <path d="M18 6H17V5H18V6Z" fill="#418805" />
    <path d="M18 5H17V4H18V5Z" fill="#3F7F07" />
    <path d="M18 4H17V3H18V4Z" fill="#5AA719" />
    <!-- ... 105 more pixels ... -->
    <path d="M18 0H20V6H18V0Z" fill="#2B6100" />
</svg>

The shimmer is a cheap trick: xpFull2.svg uses exactly the same colours as xpFull.svg, rotated 180° inside the 18 × 6 area, with the separator kept on the right. When the two frames alternate, highlights and shadows swap places, and the eye reads it as light moving across the bar. No third colour palette to design, no extra frame to maintain.

One detail that matters: SVG at integer coordinates, displayed at its native size, keeps hard pixel edges. We never scale these files; the bar is always 8 px tall in CSS.

Swapping frames with @keyframes

The track and the segments are two layers. The track is the container's own background, tiled with repeat-x, so it fills any width. The filled segments are flex children laid out left to right on top of it.

/* resources/css/app.css */
.progressBar {
    width: 100%;
    height: 8px;
    overflow: hidden;
    border-radius: 1px;
    display: flex;
    flex-direction: row;
    background-repeat: repeat-x;
    background-image: url('../img/xpEmpty.svg');
}

/* One filled segment = one 20 px frame */
.xpFull {
    width: 20px;
    height: 8px;
    animation: xpAnimation .7s infinite;
}

@keyframes xpAnimation {
    0% {
        background: url('../img/xpFull.svg');
    }
    100% {
        background: url('../img/xpFull2.svg');
    }
}

That is the whole animation. We tuned the 0.7 s duration by eye, with the game open next to the browser, until the two shimmers matched.

The detail that matters is how browsers animate between two url() values. They are not numbers, so there is no tween in the usual sense: the browser blends the two images. In our case players see a light cross-fade from frame A to frame B. Combined with the 180° rotation, it reads as a soft shimmer, close to the game's. If you want a strict pixel swap instead, make the timing explicit:

.xpFull {
    animation: xpAnimation .7s steps(1) infinite;
}

@keyframes xpAnimation {
    0%, 49.99% { background-image: url('../img/xpFull.svg'); }
    50%, 100%  { background-image: url('../img/xpFull2.svg'); }
}

We kept the cross-fade in production because it looks close to the game. This variant also uses background-image instead of the background shorthand.

Feeding the player's real values

The numbers come from the game. The JobManagement Livewire component sends a console command to the server over RCON and parses the text it gets back. The server plugin answers with a list-like string, so three regular expressions pick out the level, the current XP and the XP needed for the next level.

// app/Livewire/Dashboard/JobManagement.php
private function refreshUserJobLevels()
{
    $server = new Server(); // our RCON wrapper

    $response = $server->sendCommand('webapi jobs stats ' . auth()->user()->mojang_username);

    // XP needed for the next level: the decimal right before "]]"
    preg_match('/(\d+\.\d+)(?=\]\])/m', $response, $xpMatches);

    // Current job level: the first integer between commas
    preg_match('/,\s*(\d+),/', $response, $lvlMatches);

    // Current XP: the first decimal in the response
    preg_match('/\b(\d+\.\d+)\b/', $response, $currentMatches);

    $jobLvl = ! empty($lvlMatches) ? intval($lvlMatches[1]) : 1;
    $jobXp = ! empty($xpMatches) ? floatval($xpMatches[0]) : null;
    $currentXp = ! empty($currentMatches) ? $currentMatches[0] : null;

    $this->jobLvl = $jobLvl;
    $this->jobXp = $jobXp;
    $this->currentXp = $currentXp;
}

The bar itself is plain Blade. We turn the ratio into a number of 20 px segments, one per started 10 %, and render that many .xpFull divs. No inline width, no JS: Livewire re-renders the HTML when the values change, and the CSS animation just runs.

{{-- resources/views/livewire/dashboard/job-management.blade.php --}}
@if ($jobLvl !== null && $jobXp !== null && $currentXp !== null)
    {{-- "avant le prochain niveau" = "before the next level": the UI is in French --}}
    <p class="mb-[6px] text-white text-[14px]">
        <span class="text-base font-medium">{{ $jobXp - $currentXp }}XP</span> avant le prochain niveau
    </p>

    <div class="progressBar overflow-hidden rounded-[1px]">
        @if ($currentXp > 0)
            @for ($i = 0; $i < (ceil($currentXp / $jobXp * 100)) / 10; $i++)
                <div class="xpFull"></div>
            @endfor
        @endif
    </div>

    <div class="flex flex-row justify-between mt-1 w-full">
        <span class="text-white opacity-80">Niveau {{ $jobLvl }}</span>
        <span class="text-white opacity-80">Niveau {{ $jobLvl + 1 }}</span>
    </div>
@endif

The loop condition does the rounding: at 34 % the bound is 3.4, so the loop runs for $i = 0 to 3 and draws 4 segments. Any XP above zero shows at least one segment, which feels right to a player who has just started a level.

All segments start their animation in the same render, so they shimmer in sync, like a single bar.

Where it breaks at the edges

The bar has not caused an incident since the server opened in August 2025. Re-reading the code for this article, though, we found a handful of edges worth knowing before you copy it.

Edge case What happens What we would change
$jobXp parsed as 0.0 $currentXp / $jobXp throws DivisionByZeroError on PHP 8 and the component fails Treat $jobXp <= 0 like null and hide the bar
Player at 91 % Rounds up to 10 segments: the bar looks full before the level-up Use floor(), keeping a minimum of 1 segment when XP > 0
RCON output format The regexes depend on the plugin's text output; "first decimal = current XP" silently breaks if the order changes Ask the server team for a JSON response, or test the parser against captured outputs
Users who prefer reduced motion The shimmer never stops The media query below

The last one is a two-line fix: freeze the bar on frame A.

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
    .xpFull {
        animation: none;
        background-image: url('../img/xpFull.svg');
    }
}

None of these changes is in production yet. We list them because a reader copying the code would hit them before we do.

Wrapping up

  • A game-like UI element rarely needs a game-like engine. Two frames and a @keyframes rule were enough to make players recognise the bar.
  • Design with the build cost in mind: rotating one frame 180° gave us the shimmer without drawing a second palette.
  • Keep the logic server-side. The bar is a count of divs computed in Blade, so Livewire re-renders it like any other markup.
  • Decorative code still has edges: a zero divisor, rounding and reduced motion deserve a line each.

articles.title: I built a local-first markdown editor. Here's what kept it fast on huge docs
articles.description: Flow is a local-first markdown workspace that runs entirely in your browser. No account, no sign-up,...
articles.body_html:
Flow is a local-first markdown workspace that runs entirely in your browser. No account, no sign-up, no server holding your notes. You open it, write, and your docs stay in IndexedDB on your machine.

Live: https://markdown-editor.opalhq.fun/
Repo: https://github.com/duggal1/markdown-editor

I built it because I kept losing time to editors that asked for a login before I could type a heading, and because a lot of what I write is drafts I would rather not send anywhere. Local-first made that a property of the app instead of a line in a privacy policy.

Three engineering decisions did most of the work.

1. Virtualized preview, search in a web worker

Big docs are where most browser editors fall apart. The preview and the code pane are virtualized with TanStack Virtual, so only the rows in view are in the DOM. Updates are deferred and markdown is processed in chunks. Search and word count run in a web worker, so typing stays responsive while a large file is scanned. The editor is CodeMirror 6 with write, split and preview modes and GitHub-flavored markdown, not a homegrown engine. That saved me months.

2. Sandboxed HTML and SVG preview

Markdown allows raw HTML, which is a footgun. Inline HTML gets sanitized. A standalone HTML file renders in a sandboxed iframe with a strict content security policy. SVG preview has no script permissions. I can preview files you drop in without giving them a way to run code against the rest of the page.

3. The tiny ZIP writer behind /draw

/draw is a screenshot annotation mode. Coordinates are stored relative to the image, so annotations survive a resize. Export is JPEG, WebP, or a ZIP of everything. Instead of adding a zip library I wrote a dependency-free STORE zip writer and ran it in a worker. No compression, which is fine for screenshots, and it stayed small.

Saving is debounced IndexedDB writes with a bounded localStorage recovery copy for the case where a write dies mid-edit. PDF export is there too. The stack is React 19, TypeScript, Vite and CodeMirror 6. Built solo.

The honest tradeoff: local-first is not a backup. Your docs live in one browser's storage. Clear site data and they are gone. There is no sync and no versioned history yet. I would rather say that up front.

So, what is missing? If you open it with your largest markdown file, where does it break for you? What would you add first, and what would make you keep using an editor with no account?

articles.title: Cozy Bytes 🍺 | Rust::Who Owns the Cat? 🐈🦀
articles.description: Hoi hoi! 😸  Happy Friday! Let's learn a tiny bit of Rust! 😸🍻  No complicated architecture. No giant...
articles.body_html:
Hoi hoi! 😸

Happy Friday! Let's learn a tiny bit of Rust! 😸🍻

No complicated architecture. No giant diagrams. Just a cat, a crab, and a little bit of ownership.

Grab a beer! 🍺

🐈 Ownership::This Is My Cat!

Rust has three simple ownership rules:

  • Every value has an owner.
  • There can only be one owner at a time.
  • When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped.

Let's adopt a cat!

let a = String::from("cat");
let b = a;

println!("{b}");

📦 Move::Wait... Where's My Cat?!

What happens if we try to use a again?

println!("{a}"); // ❌ Compile error!

WHAT?! WHERE IS MY CAT?! 🙀

Ownership moved from a to b.

Sorry, a. That's not your cat anymore. 😿

Rust remembers. Rust never forgets. 🦀

🤝 Borrowing::Can I Pet Your Cat?

What if we just want to borrow a value without taking ownership?

We can use a reference (&).

let a = String::from("cat");
let b = &a;

println!("{b}");
println!("{a}");

WOW! Both work! 😸

a still owns the value. b is just borrowing it.

You can pet my cat, but you can't take it home. 😼

✏️ MutableBorrowing::The Cats Are Multiplying!

A shared reference (&) doesn't let us modify the borrowed String.

But a mutable reference (&mut) does!

let mut a = String::from("cat");

let b = &mut a;
b.push_str(" and another cat");

println!("{a}");

Output 👇

cat and another cat

Oh no.

The cats are multiplying. 🐈🐈

🦀 BorrowChecker::One Human at a Time!

Multiple humans can pet the same cat.

let cat = String::from("cat");

let a = &cat;
let b = &cat;

println!("{a} {b}"); // ✅

Everyone is happy. The cat gets extra attention. 😸

But what if two humans try to brush the same cat at once?

let mut cat = String::from("cat");

let a = &mut cat;
let b = &mut cat; // ❌ Compile error!

a.push_str(" is fluffy");
b.push_str(" is SUPER fluffy");

Rust::ABSOLUTELY NOT. 🦀💢

So here's the rule:

  • & — Many humans can borrow the cat for reading.
  • &mut — Only one human can borrow the cat for modification, with no other active borrows.

Want to brush the cat? Wait until everyone else is done borrowing it!

The crab is just trying to keep our cats safe. 🐈💚

🍪 Summary::One Little Byte at a Time

  • Ownership -> This is my cat.
  • Move -> It's your cat now.
  • & -> You can pet my cat.
  • &mut -> You can brush my cat, but one human at a time.
  • BorrowChecker -> The angry crab protecting our cats. 🦀

That's it for today's Cozy Bytes!

Rust looks scary sometimes, but we don't have to learn everything at once.

One little byte at a time. 😸💚

Happy Friday! 🍻

articles.title: Everybody Has an AI Apocalypse Story. Almost Nobody Reads the Fine Print.
