articles.body_html:
Think back to the first time you pictured AI.

Maybe it was HAL's calm red eye refusing to open the pod bay doors. Maybe it was the Terminator. Maybe you never saw either one and still knew the story anyway, because it's everywhere: we build the machine, the machine wakes up, and the machine comes for us.

Whether you watched the movies or not, that's the picture a lot of us grew up with. Robot means threat. In 2022, people in San Francisco put it right on a banner.

San Francisco City Hall, December 5, 2022, protesting a vote to let police use robots with deadly force. Photo: Pax Ahimsa Gethen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

So here's the question I keep asking. Of protesters, of headlines, of the people building it: how exactly does AI end the world? Not the movie version. The real one. What happens first, and where's the proof?

Most of the time, nobody gives me details. And when the insiders do, what I get is a scenario, not proof.

What they say they're building

Here's what surprised me. The people building AI don't describe a movie. They describe something closer to paradise. In their own words:

  • Dario Amodei, Anthropic: "my basic prediction is that AI-enabled biology and medicine will allow us to compress the progress that human biologists would have achieved over the next 50-100 years into 5-10 years." He describes what's coming as a "country of geniuses in a datacenter." (Machines of Loving Grace, October 2024)
  • Sam Altman, OpenAI: "In the 2030s, intelligence and energy—ideas, and the ability to make ideas happen—are going to become wildly abundant." (The Gentle Singularity)
  • Mark Zuckerberg, Meta: "Meta's vision is to bring personal superintelligence to everyone." (Personal Superintelligence)
  • xAI, Elon Musk's company, on its own page: "Accelerate human scientific discovery. We build AI to understand the universe."
  • Demis Hassabis, Google DeepMind: "Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), a system that exhibits all the cognitive capabilities the brain has, is probably only a few short years away." Same essay: "advances on the frontier are outpacing our understanding of the technology." (A Framework for Frontier AI and the Dawning of a New Age, July 14, 2026)
  • Jensen Huang, NVIDIA's founder: "AI will transform every industry, power every company, and be built by every country." (July 24, 2026)
  • Satya Nadella, Microsoft: "In my view, our priority has to be building a frontier ecosystem, not just a frontier model, so value flows broadly across every company, every industry, and every country." (A frontier without an ecosystem is not stable, June 14, 2026)

A century of medicine in a decade. Abundance. A superintelligence for everyone. AI in every industry. Understanding the universe. Hold onto that, because some of the same people have also signed their names to warnings that sound nothing like it.

Warnings, not proof

On March 22, 2023, the Future of Life Institute published a letter calling on "all AI labs to immediately pause for at least 6 months the training of AI systems more powerful than GPT-4." Elon Musk signed it. On the list when I checked, his name was third, as "CEO of SpaceX, Tesla & Twitter."

112 days later, xAI's own company page lists its "Company announcement," July 12, 2023. Today that same page advertises Colossus: "200K GPUs. Built in 122 days."

Sign the pause. Start a new AI company 112 days later.

He's not the only one. In 2023, the Statement on AI Risk said: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." Among the signers: Sam Altman, "CEO, OpenAI." Dario Amodei, "CEO, Anthropic." Demis Hassabis, "CEO, Google DeepMind." That's the whole statement. One sentence. The people running three leading AI labs put their names under the word extinction, and then kept building.

To be fair, some of them do describe how it could go wrong. Amodei's own essay walks through scenarios: AI helping someone build a biological weapon, AI systems whose own goals turn out to be hostile to ours, authoritarian governments using it to surveil and repress. Those are worth taking seriously. But a scenario isn't proof. The question I never hear answered is how likely each one is, what evidence backs it, and whether a given law would actually stop it.

And when they write at length, they hedge. Sam Altman, in The Gentle Singularity: "There will be very hard parts like whole classes of jobs going away, but on the other hand the world will be getting so much richer so quickly that we'll be able to seriously entertain new policy ideas we never could before." The world getting richer is not the same as the person who lost the job being okay. That second part is the one that needs proof, the same as the warnings do.

There's another question underneath the job fear: if a machine can do your work, does that make your life worth less? I can't fathom believing that. Your value was never your job title. Paying the bills matters, which is why replacing work without giving people a way to live isn't freedom. But if people's needs are met while AI carries more of the work, think about what that opens up: time to learn, to build, to care for each other, and to figure out what you actually want to dedicate yourself to. Work can give life meaning. It doesn't have to be the only place we find it.

A warning doesn't have to be proof. But it does have to show its evidence, its uncertainty, and why the proposed response fits the risk. Without that, it's a feeling. And feelings can end up with real power.

I learned that one in person. Some friends introduced me to someone running for office, so I asked what policies they were looking into. As close as I can remember it, the answer was: "Ha, you got me there. I don't know." I laughed and said I wasn't trying to catch anybody out. Then they looked me over and said I looked like someone who's for data centers. I said, so what if I am? That was the end of it. They told their friend to stay away from me, I was for data centers, and they walked off.

They won. That night I didn't hear a single policy, just a feeling, and now that person has a real vote.

The warnings, quoted in a bill

Dario Amodei runs Anthropic, one of the biggest AI companies in the world. In his January 2026 essay he calls job loss "a topic that I warned about very publicly in 2025, where I predicted that AI could displace half of all entry-level white collar jobs in the next 1–5 years, even as it accelerates economic growth and scientific progress."

Here's how Bernie Sanders' AI Data Center Moratorium Act quotes him, as a reason to stop building:

Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, who predicted that "AI could displace half of all entry-level white collar jobs in the next 1 to 5 years." and that "humanity is about to be handed almost unimaginable power, and it is deeply unclear whether our social, political, and technological systems possess the maturity to wield it."

The bill keeps both warnings and drops the growth.

To be fair, the warning is real. Losing half the entry-level jobs would be serious either way, and growth doesn't cancel that out. But the bill quoted the scary half of the man's sentence and left the rest on the floor. Its House version, H.R. 9442 from Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, builds its case mostly out of the builders' own predictions and plans: Musk, Amodei, Bezos, Gates and others, with five billionaires' net worths printed right in the findings. The way I see it, the fear Congress is quoting came from the people selling the product.

What would the bills actually do? Stop "the construction or upgrading of new or existing artificial intelligence data centers" until Congress passes laws requiring, among other things: federal review of AI products before release, data centers that don't "increase utility or electricity bills of consumers," communities empowered to "approve or reject" each project, no government subsidies, union jobs. Then a law has to expressly end the freeze. There's no end date of its own. It doesn't order running data centers to shut down. Neither bill is law.

It isn't one party, either. Republican Sen. Josh Hawley and Democrat Richard Blumenthal introduced the GRID Act on February 11, 2026, "requiring data centers to use energy from sources that are separate from the U.S. grid and publicly report their electricity usage." Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, September 21, 2026: "Data centers must pay their own way, protect our grid and water, and complete the ERCOT and TWDB audits. Until they do, TCEQ will issue no permits sought by data center projects."

Strip away the apocalypse talk and the one place left and right clearly overlap is the power bill.

South Minneapolis, November 6, 2026. Photo: Chad Davis, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

What doing it right looks like

This was never about picking a side. It's about doing it right, and doing it right means two things: the costs land where they belong, and people can see what's going on.

The first part already exists. On July 9, 2025, Ohio's utility regulator adopted AEP Ohio's data center tariff, covering new data centers and expansions of 25 megawatts or more. It doesn't ban anything. In plain terms:

  • They sign long contracts. Up to 12 years: a ramp-up of no more than four years, plus eight.
  • They have to grow into what they reserved. During the ramp, their contracted capacity can't sit below 50% in year one, 65% in year two, 80% in year three and 90% in year four.
  • They pay for what they reserved, even if they don't use it. Their monthly billing demand, the kilowatts they're billed for (not the dollar amount), can't drop below the greater of 85% of their highest billing demand in the past 11 months, or a minimum based on the size of their contract.
  • They can't just walk away. Leave early, after the fifth year following the ramp, and the exit fee is 36 months of minimum charges after they give notice.

As I read it, that shifts much more of the risk onto the data center itself, instead of leaving ordinary customers exposed if the promised demand never shows up. It's not the whole answer. Virginia's legislative study office, JLARC, found in 2024 that "current rates appropriately allocate costs to the customers responsible for incurring them, including data center customers," and still projected that a typical Dominion residential customer could see generation and transmission costs rise by an estimated $14 to $37 a month by 2040, in 2024 dollars, because the whole system is growing. Both can be true: the data center pays its share, and your bill can still go up.

And the water? Berkeley Lab's 2024 report estimates U.S. data centers directly consumed about 66 billion liters in 2023, and that the power plants supplying them used nearly 800 billion liters more. That's a national number, though. It can't tell a town whether its creek runs lower in August. Local harm needs local data.

For perspective, put those numbers next to other big resource users. The EPA says Americans use nearly 8 billion gallons of water a day outdoors at home, mainly for landscape irrigation; its page doesn't give a year. Berkeley Lab's 2023 estimate for data centers' direct water works out to about 48 million gallons a day. Those two aren't measured exactly the same way: the EPA counts water used, and Berkeley Lab counts water consumed, the part that doesn't go back. So I won't pretend the gap is a precise multiple. But it's worth knowing which number is in the billions. Worldwide, farming accounts for 69 percent of freshwater withdrawals, according to the UN's FAO, though it notes a few countries with very high withdrawals pull that up; averaged country by country, it's 59 percent. On power, the IEA projects data centers will reach about 3% of the world's electricity by 2030. Air conditioners and fans were already using about 10% back in 2018.

None of that makes data centers free. It means they belong in the same scrutiny we give every major resource user: what each one consumes, where the pressure falls, what benefit it provides, and who pays. Being familiar shouldn't earn something a pass, and being new shouldn't decide the verdict.

The second part is transparency, and it's further behind. The EU already requires covered data centers to report energy and sustainability indicators to a European database. What I want goes further: people should know what these buildings are for. Where the data is going, and what's coming out of it. We're heading toward algorithms that know us better than we know ourselves, deciding what shows up on our feeds, and a lot of that is already here. If a building is going to power that, the people living next to it deserve the same clear answers we'd demand from a power plant.

It isn't a calculator

None of this means we should shame people for how they use it. A kid making a goofy cat picture isn't doing anything wrong. A family photo can mean everything to the person who made it.

But it isn't a calculator either. The International Energy Agency's 2026 report says a simple text question now typically uses less electricity than running a television for the same amount of time, but video, reasoning and agent tasks "can consume hundreds or thousands of times more energy per query than simple text generation." Researchers at Hugging Face and Carnegie Mellon who measured 88 models found that general-purpose generative systems "are orders of magnitude more expensive than task-specific systems."

What's missing is a standard for how we work alongside it. Not rules about what you're allowed to make. Just knowing what a request actually costs, the way you'd know what your car burns, and choosing with that in mind. Make the cost visible, make it land where it belongs, and let people decide with their eyes open. Freedom, with the bill attached.

Everybody's reacting

The reaction is everywhere. On November 14, 2026, protesters marched at OpenAI's headquarters as part of actions in about 20 cities; the Latin Times counted roughly 150 in San Francisco. Data Center Watch counts 843 opposition groups in 49 states, and says community opposition blocked or delayed 45 projects worth about $68 billion in just April through June of 2026, according to Bloomberg.

The March for an AI Treaty in Manhattan, November 14, 2026. Photo: Tessa Bury, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Christian County, Illinois, September 26, 2026. Photo: User:Visviva, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

On November 19, 2026, the day Anthropic started trading on Nasdaq (yes, the company whose AI helped me write this), police took four people into custody after a smaller group sat in front of the Nasdaq entrance in Times Square and refused to move. On X, the account that posted the video, @ScooterCasterNY, called them "Anti-AI Protesters" in one post and "Anti-ICE protesters" in the post it quoted. amNY names several groups, including Stop Funding Billionaires, Climate Defiance, Sunrise NYC and ACT UP NYC, with concerns from pension funds to AI partnerships with law enforcement, "particularly those involving Palantir and ICE." One protest, two labels. Most people will only ever see one of them.

It reaches small towns too. In my own city, AI-generated artwork showed up on Nashua's solar-powered trash cans in August 2025. A member of the city's Board of Public Works asked publicly, "What do we gain by handing these areas over to Ai?" Later, someone spray-painted "HIRE REAL ARTISTS" across one of them. I saw it myself.

It isn't only protesters, either. Plenty of programmers feel it too. This week a video went around for any old-school programmer who hates AI. It's from @bennett.reloaded, painted in thick brushstrokes: a programmer named Dave at his bookshelf, and a chart running from punch cards in the 1950s to Python in 1991, every row another way to make the computer say hi. Then: "Fine. But easier means hidden." His answer: "No. I started because I was twelve." And the question at the center of it: "What if I don't want to?"

That's a fair question, and it's a specific one. It's about what you lose when the work gets hidden, not about robots ending the world.

Here's what I noticed, and it cuts against my own side. The fights that were specific actually won things. Video game voice and motion actors went on strike for 11 months, and in July 2025 they ratified a contract with 95% voting yes that requires their consent before a company makes a digital replica of them. They knew exactly what they were afraid of and asked for exactly that. Even the graffiti says something specific: hire people.

A demand you can explain can win. A feeling just gets louder.

The half of the movie we forgot

Remember those movies from the start? Here's the part most of us skipped.

Ask people what happens in I, Robot and they'll tell you the robots take over. That's half the story. Will Smith's detective hates robots because one pulled him out of a car crash and let a 12-year-old girl in the other car drown, based on cold logic and odds of survival. It did the math. It didn't judge. The villain, VIKI, does the same thing at scale: her own "evolved interpretation" of the Three Laws decides humanity has to be controlled to be protected from itself. And the hero? Sonny, the one robot built with the ability to choose whether to follow the Three Laws at all. The machine that could say no is the one that helps stop her.

Steven Spielberg's A.I. Artificial Intelligence goes further. The most monstrous thing in it isn't a machine. It's the Flesh Fair, where obsolete robots are destroyed in front of jeering crowds. The crowd only turns when David, a robot boy built to love, begs for his life.

And it isn't only in the movies. In October 2025, an AI gun-detection system at Kenwood High School in Baltimore County flagged a student's bag of chips as a gun. Four of the teens are now suing. According to their complaint, the system flagged it "with 90% confidence," and within two minutes, designated school and police representatives "reviewed the Alert, determined there was no gun, and canceled it." More than ten minutes after that, the complaint says, the principal sent a screenshot of the alert to the school resource officer without checking whether it had been canceled, and that set off an armed police response. The four were "ordered to their knees, handcuffed and searched, despite no wrongdoing," TheGrio reported.

That's the robot in the car, in real life. The machine did the math. People reviewed it, used judgment, and canceled the alert. Armed police still showed up.

Watch them all the way through and a lot of these movies aren't warning us about intelligence. They're warning us about rules without judgment, and about what people do when they're scared. We just remember the explosions.

That's what's insane to me. Out of everything in this world, humans draw the line on intelligence right where it grows a backbone.

The oldest version of the story

So why bring up a clay giant in a piece about data centers? Because it's one of the oldest AI stories there is. Long before computers, people imagined building a man out of clay and bringing it to life with a holy name, and they were already working out what goes wrong. If the movies are where a lot of us learned to fear AI, the golem is where that fear goes back to. And it teaches the same lesson the movies do once you finish them.

Poster for Der Golem (1920), by Hans Poelzig. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

In the Talmud, in Sanhedrin 65b, the rabbi Rava creates a man and sends him to Rabbi Zeira. Rabbi Zeira speaks to him, and he does not reply. So Rabbi Zeira says, "Return to your dust." In a sixteenth-century telling collected in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, the golem grows into a monster its maker fears might destroy the world, until he pulls the Shem, the holy name, from its forehead. In another version, recorded in the Encyclopaedia Judaica, the word emet, truth, is written on its forehead, and erasing one letter leaves met, death.

None of these stories says the golem thought for itself. In the Talmud it can't even answer a question. The way I read it, that's an echo chamber made of clay: something that carries out what it's given without ever understanding it. Same as the robot in the car. And in the later telling, what stops it isn't a war. It's its own maker. The power and the off switch lived in the same hands the whole time.

AI isn't clay, and the point isn't that today's AI is a golem. The point is that we've been telling this story for about 1,500 years, and we keep fearing the wrong part of it. To me, the danger was never a mind that can say no. It's one that obeys perfectly and understands nothing, and makers who forget the switch is theirs to hold. We have to learn from that story and make sure we don't die from truth.

How I got here

I didn't start with this conclusion. I started by stripping everything apart and setting aside what I thought I knew. First principles.

  1. Read the originals, not the coverage. The essays. Both bills, all 13 pages. The tariff. The lawsuit.
  2. Check every quote against the page it came from. That's how the half sentence showed up.
  3. Check what every number actually counts. A national water number isn't your town's creek. A scenario isn't a probability.
  4. Ask who's paying, for the building, the power and the quote.
  5. Get checked by someone looking for your mistakes. Two other AI systems went through it looking for mine. They found plenty, and I fixed what they found.

Here's what would prove me wrong. If entry-level white-collar jobs collapse and the people who lose them never share in the growth, Amodei's warning wins, and a richer world won't mean much to them. And if the people fighting these buildings can already tell you what the bills do and which half of Amodei's sentence got cut, then I'm wrong about this debate. I haven't run that survey. I've only read the sentences. The sentences were cut. That part I can show you.

You can do the same with anything you read about AI, including this. Ask yourself: How do I know this? Why do I know this? Is it me thinking, or something I was handed?

We all saw the movie. Closing the gap doesn't take a degree. It takes reading the whole sentence, and watching the whole movie.

So I'll ask you: what's one thing about AI you believed for years, and where did you actually get it from?

Sources (all linked above): FLI pause letter · xAI company page · Statement on AI Risk · Altman, The Gentle Singularity · Amodei, Machines of Loving Grace · Zuckerberg, Personal Superintelligence · Hassabis, A Framework for Frontier AI · Huang, July 24, 2026 · Nadella, A frontier without an ecosystem is not stable · Amodei, The Adolescence of Technology · Sanders draft bill · H.R. 9442 · Hawley–Blumenthal GRID Act · Gov. articles.title: I Haven't Written a Line of Code in Months. And I Don't Know How to Feel About It.
articles.description: Introduction   It's been a while since I wrote something here. It feels like it was a...
articles.body_html:
Introduction

It's been a while since I wrote something here. It feels like it was a lifetime ago. Our world, and especially our programming world, moves so fast that I can't recognize the way it was 6 years ago, 2 years ago, or even at the beginning of this year. So, I wanted to write down some thoughts and see where they take me.

Dealing with changes

In our line of work, we're used to changes right? New languages, new technologies, new frameworks... we've always had new things to look forward to, or being scared of, learn, hate... But this AI stuff... Damn, it's not just something new, it's the first time I've actually felt threatened, in danger, overwhelmed.

It's a very strange feeling because I have the feeling like we are at the edge of a new world, full of possibilities, adventures, discoveries. Things that we thought would take us weeks, months, or years to do or solve become doable so much faster. In the field of science, we see cool stuff happening. And even if I don't understand anything about it, it looks cool to discover new proofs and solutions, even if it's AI assisted. But...

What about me?

I'm a good developer ok? I'm not a rockstar, but I've some strenghts. I've always enjoyed learning new stuff about design patterns, how to write good code. Less than a year ago, I was still learning new things, trying to write more elegant code. I was happy when I found a beautiful solution to a problem.

Around March this year, our team decided it was time to equip everyone with Claude. I don't think I've written a line of code since then. How insane is that? Most of my time was spent in writing code, and now, it has completely disappeared from my tasks. So now, I'm mostly managing agents and doing all the conception and planning. That's where my "expertise" comes in. Because this stuff writes much better code than me anyway.

I feel... dizzy.

What about my (our) future?

The one thing that is scary is not knowing to me. I don't know what our jobs will look like next year, in 2 years, in 10 years. Will we still have a job? How will it look? I'm not much into the doom prediction like "Developers will be gone in 6 months". But something is gonna change drastically right? What about the juniors, the people entering the job market today?

It's not all bad of course. It's not. It's the uncertainty that's difficult for me.

I'm building a very cool project with a few colleagues and AI allowed us to move a lot faster than we would have on our own. That's really exciting. Being able to deliver features a lot faster to users is always a nice feeling. That's one of the main reasons I started doing this anyway, help people.

Loss of craftsmanship

When I wrote the code, with my slow hands, I felt like a craftsman. I was building something. The code was mine. Now, it's not. It's industrialized. A machine makes it. Like countless other craftsmen in the history of our species, what I used to do with my hands in hours or days is done by a machine in minutes.

It's a strange feeling. Of course, I try to comfort myself. I still need to pilot this thing. It doesn't have my humanity, it doesn't know my users like I know them. I have better business knowledge than this machine. And in the end, it's always me that makes the final decision. For how long? And how much value does it have?

This is also why I write this. Because I can still sit in front of my computer and pour out the words. My words. From my brain and my heart. It feels good to create something all by yourself. And I still have the hope that whatever the future holds for us, we will build cool stuff to help people. I hope that the AI era that we're entering will be a net positive for humanity.

Conclusion

That's it, that was my little rant. I'll keep building things that I believe will help people to better their lives and jobs. We will see, together, where this new world takes us.

Have fun <3

Introduction

In this article, I'll expose an issue we had in one of my freelance missions, what we learned from it and how it started our journey towards building our own system.

Disclaimer: I am one of the co-founders of Notifizz, a unified notification platform that leverages AI to give marketing teams autonomy in handling their notifications.

The problem

Our architecture was composed of several microservices. One of them was handling the notifications: receiving requests and calling whatever third party service was responsible for sending a message.

Marketing teams designed notifications to achieve certain goals: alerting a customer of a new invoice, reminding him of an important task, informing about a new functionality... Each notification exists , or should exist, to achieve a business goal.

Obviously, there is no guarantee that a notification will allow the company to achieve whatever goal they set right away. You track an objective related to a notification, and you see if users do the action you intended them to do from that notification.

What if it doesn't work? Or doesn't work well enough? Marketing might want to make a few changes. Adjust the wording. Perhaps send the notification at a different moment in the process. Or maybe send an email AND an in-app message...

And that's the first hurdle. For every change, marketing needs to either have a little bit of experience with certain tools (we used mailgun for example, which isn't the most straightforward piece of technology for non-devs) or send a ticket to the dev team to implement the changes. The marketing team is completely dependent on the dev team. It loses time and possibly keeps a suboptimal campaign live while the dev team finds the time to do the changes and push it to prod.

A solution?

So we thought (back in 2023), what if the marketing team had complete control over their campaigns? What if they were completely independent from the dev team? How would that look like?

You still need developers in the loop, obviously. But we thought that we could create everything we needed in our application beforehand (events, endpoints...) like building blocks, and let the marketing team construct their campaigns like this.

Our application would emit events. For instance, a new invoice is created -> event invoice.created, emitted from the microservice responsible for invoicing. That microservice would publish this event and its payload to a pub/sub topic.

So far, so good. But now you need an interface right? Because marketing wants to create a campaign to alert clients about the invoice. And the marketing team doesn't know anything about code, or what's an API or a microservice... And they need something flexible so that they add a new field if necessary, or update the wording...

So we thought about adding Make. Make lets you create scenarios and chain modules in a sequence. It takes an input (in our case, it would take our pub/sub' subscription) and you can chain different modules to manipulate data.

And because you can create custom modules in Make, we created modules that allowed us to call our API, so we could enrich the original event payload input with data from some of our other microservices. That way, we thought, even if marketing is missing a field, they will use one of our pre-designed modules and add it themselves, without the devs! Genius!

Right? Input's data -> call one or several modules to enrich -> call our notification microservice to send the notification.

Well, it was a disaster.

Why it didn't work

First, the payload you get from the event is a JSON, and it needs to be parsed for the Make scenario to know it and manipulate it. So right off the bat, you're adding a JSON concept into a process that's supposed to be developers free.

Second, if you call our API, you need to think about security. So you need to pass a token, or an api key or something from Make to make sure your data is not being called from anyone. Another concept that's not marketing friendly.

Third, you actually need a lot of JSON manipulating in that use case inside Make. Too much for a non technical person to use. The whole point was to make sure you didn't need to be a developer to use that process.

A "simple" scenario could look like this

Fourth, the variety of tools used complicated things. Because everything was spread out across different tools (templates were in Mailgun, the team used Intercom, Mailchimp, plus Make ...), it was impossible to teach the marketing team to be fully autonomous in the process. It would have been way too costly to train them on these tools to handle everything like we expected. It wasn't their job anyway.

Fifth, we also needed to handle different environments. Obviously, you don't send your notifications to production right off the bat. You need to test them locally, then test them in a deployed environment then finally you push it to production. In our case, we needed to have a different scenario for each environment (different pub/sub subscription/topic, different modules).

What we learned

Lack of control

No-code, at least in 2023 the way we used it became a growing problem saying: You need to adapt everything to us and our way of things, not the other way around. And it became clear that the level of complexity would be way too expensive to implement and maintain with the available tools in order to achieve the marketing autonomy goals we had.

The expertise needed

You can't remove developers entirely from that loop. At one point or another, you need a developer to implement some code (an endpoint to enrich, a new event, a new field in an existing event ...). So the problem became more of: how do we clearly separate dev tasks from marketing tasks so that each team does what it's good at, without making each other lose too much time?

To do that, we think, we need to have a centralized interface where everything was easier to follow and monitor. In one place, designing your email, in-app or intercom messages, track deliverability, events and their payloads and where in the development process is the campaign.

Lack of visibility

Marketing teams have very little visibility on the number of notifications that are being sent throughout the application and in other marketing campaigns. We realized that our marketing team knew quite well about the actions they took to bring in new clients but very little about the users inside the app. And that was mostly due to the fact that there were a lot of different tools involved. The development team became, de facto, responsible for a lot of notifications inside the app, from designing, to wording, to tracking its effects.

Conclusion

This is what started our journey into building Notifizz. There is no doubt that what we did at the time was not perfect. Decisions were taken that could have been better. Technical choices that could have been wrong. In the end, the system worked, but couldn't work for the audience we had in mind. But it opened new doors, with the idea that maybe we could do better by building our own product.

articles.title: Anthropic IPO: what the prospectus says about rate limits and compute
articles.description: Anthropic's IPO prospectus says it has changed rate limits before and may again. Day-one prices, the lock-up, the $900.9B compute bill and one cancellable contract.
articles.body_html:
Anthropic began trading on Nasdaq on Thursday, November 19, 2026 under the symbol ANT. The first trade was $111.50, the close was $97.17, and the final prospectus contains a sentence that matters to anyone who builds on Claude: the company says it has changed usage limits and rate limits before and may change them again. This article covers what the day-one numbers show, who was allowed to sell shares, what the Anthropic IPO prospectus says about rate limits and compute, and one contract in the filing that either side can already cancel. It accompanies today's Daily Diff episode.

TL;DR

  • Anthropic priced its IPO at $83.00 on November 18, sold 980 million Class A shares (Anthropic), and opened trading at $111.50 on Thursday. The close was $97.17, 17 percent above the offer price. The lowest price of the session was $92.72.
  • Valuation figures differ by share count: CNBC says about $1.8 trillion at the close and Forbes says $1.27 trillion.
  • The prospectus lets non-founder directors, officers and employees sell up to 315 million shares from the first trading day. It says they may. It does not say anyone did.
  • In its risk factors Anthropic writes that it has changed, and may in the future change, usage limits, rate limits, or model and product capabilities.
  • Anthropic says it has about $900.9 billion of compute and infrastructure commitments, $70.7 billion of them due within twelve months. One $34.9 billion Lambda agreement is "currently terminable by either party".
  • My verdict is NEEDS REVIEW: keep building on Claude and keep a second model wired in.

What did the Anthropic IPO do on day one?

The offer price was $83.00, above the $70 to $78 range the company had filed on November 10, according to the prospectus history that CNBC and Reuters summarise.

Yahoo Finance, Nasdaq, CNBC, Forbes and Reuters agree on these numbers:

Item Price
Offer $83.00
First trade $111.50 (+34 % over the offer)
Day high $115.10
Day low $92.72
Close $97.17 (+17 % over the offer)

Two readings follow from the table. The stock never traded below the offer price during the regular session, so anyone who bought at $83 was ahead all day. And it closed about 13 percent below the first trade, so anyone who bought at the open was behind. Reuters describes the early exuberance as fading. I am quoting day one only. The second session was already trading while this article was written, and a price here would be stale.

Which market value is right?

Three outlets give three figures for the close. CNBC says Anthropic closed with a market cap of about $1.8 trillion. Forbes lists $1.27 trillion at the close. Reuters writes that its $2 trillion figure at the debut is fully diluted and includes options and restricted stock units that have not vested, and that the value on outstanding shares reached as much as $1.5 trillion. The prospectus counts 13,219,642,274 Class A and Class N shares after the offering and the concurrent private placement, and 13.22 billion shares times $97.17 is about $1.28 trillion.

Bessemer's Byron Deeter, whose firm is an Anthropic investor, told CNBC: "They could have priced the IPO higher. At every financing they have chosen to leave some money on the table." Bessemer is an Anthropic investor, so read the comment as an insider's view of the pricing.

Who was allowed to sell Anthropic shares on day one?

The prospectus describes lock-up and market standoff agreements covering about 15.5 billion shares. Most existing holders are restricted for up to 180 days, and the co-founders and certain holders of more than 0.5 percent of fully diluted shares for up to 365 days. The release schedule has exceptions. On the first trading day, non-founder directors, officers and current and former employees and consultants are eligible to sell up to 315 million Class A shares. That is about a third of the 980 million shares the IPO sold. A second tranche of up to 303 million shares is scheduled for the 27th day after the prospectus date, December 15, 2026, and larger waves follow around its earnings releases and at the 180th and 365th days. The concurrent private placement shares, about $26 billion of Class N stock, are not subject to the lock-up.

"Eligible to sell" is the filing's wording. The filing does not say that anyone sold, and I did not find a source that does.

What does the Anthropic prospectus say about rate limits?

If you build on Claude, this is the part of the filing I would read twice. In the risk factors, Anthropic writes: "We have also changed, and may in the future change, usage limits, rate limits, or model and product capabilities, which could adversely affect our reputation and the perceived value of our offerings. Some of these changes have resulted, and could in the future result, in claims that our disclosures regarding model access or capabilities were inadequate or misleading."

Two points on reading it. First, this is standard risk-factor language: a company lists what could go wrong, and the sentence is not an announcement of cuts. Second, it is also a plain statement of fact about the past: limits have changed before. The same section says that concerns about model safety, interpretability, alignment and welfare may lead Anthropic to limit or delay the deprecation of older models and to keep supporting legacy versions, which creates tradeoffs in "compute distribution".

The practical consequence is architectural. If your product depends on one model at one limit, a limit change is an outage you did not plan for. Queue and retry with backoff, keep the model name in configuration, and test a second provider path before you need it. That advice is mine; the filing does not give it.

Why does the compute bill matter for developers?

Capacity is what rate limits are made of. The prospectus says that as of and after September 30, 2026, Anthropic has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements, including short-term commitments and leases not yet commenced, with an aggregate committed spend of approximately $900.9 billion. About $451.6 billion is expected before the end of 2030, and about $70.7 billion is due in the twelve months after September 30. For comparison, the filing reports revenue of $33.2 billion for the nine months to September 30, 2026, up from $2.5 billion a year earlier, and an operating loss of $1.3 billion.

A Futurum analyst told CNBC that demand is running ahead of supply, so missing capacity turns into lost revenue very quickly. He also said a serious shortage is unlikely, because Anthropic's biggest suppliers are also its biggest investors. CNBC adds that Anthropic has said long-term capacity is significantly cheaper than short-term commitments, which it would need when demand exceeds its long-term capacity.

Which contract can already be cancelled?

The Lambda agreements are the open item. Anthropic agreed in May, June and August 2026 to spend about $41.3 billion with Lambda for access to NVIDIA GPU compute. About $34.9 billion of that is the August agreement, and the filing says: "either party may terminate if Lambda does not secure the facility lease by a specific date. Lambda did not secure the facility lease by such date and, as a result, the August 2026 agreement is currently terminable by either party. Neither party has delivered notice of termination as of the date of this prospectus, and we do not currently intend to terminate the agreement."

That contract is about four percent of the total commitments ($34.9 billion of $900.9 billion). It does not show that capacity is short. It shows one deal where a supplier missed a condition, and a company that says it does not plan to walk away.

Also today: did Claude solve two black-hole problems?

Anthropic published a research post on November 17 saying Claude solved two open problems in the physics of black holes. According to the post, a researcher asked Claude for open problems, it returned 22 candidates, and separate agents worked on them in the background for about six weeks, reading each other's progress posts. One result completes a three-loop calculation set up in 2003 and finds that the transition is abrupt at weak coupling in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. The other finds the exact limit of the simplest modular bootstrap, about 9.13, where the best earlier proof was 8.5.

Anthropic says almost every piece of the first calculation was done twice by agents acting independently, that the results were formally verified in the Lean proof checker in September, and that a physicist checked every main result. The two preprints are on Hexagon, a repository that says it does not perform peer review, and Hexagon labels them "Primarily AI-generated text" with "Human understanding: some parts". Anthropic says neither result describes our universe directly or has practical applications. I could not find an independent expert review yet. For developers the reusable part is the harness: many agents, shared notes, every number computed twice and a checker at the end.

Also today: OpenSSL CVE-2026-121481 scores 9.8, and OpenSSL says Low

CVE-2026-121481 is an integer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock(), OpenSSL's base64 encoder: with an input length close to the largest signed integer, the output-size calculation overflows and the function writes past the caller's buffer. The 9.8 CRITICAL score on the NVD record comes from CISA's enrichment container. OpenSSL's own CVE record rates the issue Low, says "No path by which an attacker can trigger this has been identified", and explains that its TLS, QUIC and CMS code never encode buffers that large.

The reporter says a command-line route exists. In the review of the fix pull request, reviewer Bob Beck wrote that the report's reproducer is "completely synthetic, and probably should not be a CVE without evidence it really happens". On November 20, OpenSSL team member Matt Caswell wrote that using OPENSSL_assert in the library is "a DoS waiting to happen". The pull request is open. The record lists versions before 4.0.4 and 4.1.1 as affected, and neither release has been published. CISA's own exploitation tag reads "none". If your code passes an externally controlled length to that function, bound the length before the call.

Verdict: NEEDS REVIEW

The market paid up on day one. The filing also says the capacity behind the product is still being built, that limits have moved before, and that one large supply contract can already be cancelled. I would keep building on Claude and keep a second model wired in. I gave the S-1 the same stamp in October.

FAQ

What did Anthropic's stock do on its first day?

It priced at $83.00, traded first at $111.50, reached $115.10, fell to a low of $92.72 and closed at $97.17, 17 percent above the offer price.

Can Anthropic employees sell shares right away?

The prospectus lets non-founder directors, officers and current and former employees and consultants sell up to 315 million shares from the first trading day. Most other holders are locked up for 180 or 365 days.

Does the Anthropic prospectus say rate limits will change?

It says Anthropic has changed usage limits and rate limits before and may change them in the future, and that some changes led to claims about its disclosures.

Is OpenSSL CVE-2026-121481 critical?

CISA's enrichment scores it 9.8, and OpenSSL's own record rates it Low because no attacker-controlled path to the overflow is known.

Sources
