articles.title: 10 Things Every Coder Has Blamed at Least Once (at least I have)
articles.description: There's one sentence every developer has probably said at some point:  "But it was working five...
articles.body_html:
There's one sentence every developer has probably said at some point:

"But it was working five minutes ago!"

And then begins the investigation.

You check the code.

You restart the application.

You read the error message.

You search Stack Overflow.

You ask AI.

You restart everything again.

And when nothing works, you begin looking for someone—or something—to blame.

I've been there.

Sometimes the problem really is the framework, the dependency, or the server.

And sometimes?

Well, we'll get to that.

Here are ten things I think almost every coder has blamed at least once.

1. The Compiler: "It's Clearly a Compiler Problem"

You write a perfectly reasonable piece of code.

At least, it looks reasonable to you.

The compiler disagrees.

Suddenly, your terminal is filled with errors that seem to have been written by someone who is personally disappointed in you.

You stare at the screen.

You check the syntax.

You question your life choices.

Then you discover you've forgotten a bracket.

One bracket.

Thirty minutes of frustration.

And somehow, the compiler is still the villain.

Because why couldn't it just understand what you meant?

2. The Internet: The Universal Suspect

Application not loading?

Internet problem.

Package installation failed?

Internet problem.

API request timing out?

Definitely the internet.

There's something comforting about blaming the connection.

It's an external problem.

It's outside our control.

And most importantly, it means we don't have to question our code.

At least not immediately.

Then you discover the API endpoint is wrong.

The internet was innocent.

Again.

3. The Cache: "Have You Tried Clearing It?"

The application has been updated.

The bug has been fixed.

The new CSS looks perfect.

But the browser is still showing the old version.

You refresh.

Nothing.

You refresh harder, as if the browser can sense your frustration.

Nothing.

You open an incognito window.

Suddenly, everything works.

The cache has entered the chat.

And once you've been betrayed by caching, it becomes your prime suspect in every future debugging session.

Sometimes correctly.

Sometimes not.

But the accusation is always ready.

4. The Framework: "This Wouldn't Happen in Another Language"

Every developer has experienced that moment when a framework seems determined to make a simple task complicated.

You want to display a button.

Somehow, you're now reading documentation about lifecycle hooks, dependency injection, build configurations, and seventeen different ways to manage state.

At some point, you start thinking:

"Why am I using this framework?"

Then you search for alternatives.

You discover another framework.

It looks cleaner.

Simpler.

More elegant.

For approximately three days.

Then you encounter its problems.

And the cycle begins again.

Sometimes changing frameworks is just changing the location of your frustration.

5. The Documentation: "Who Wrote This?"

Ah, documentation.

That magical place where everything is explained—except the one thing you're trying to do.

You search for an example.

The documentation gives you a conceptual overview.

You search for the function.

It explains what the function does.

You search for an actual implementation.

It redirects you to another page.

That page links to a tutorial.

The tutorial uses an older version.

And the API you need was deprecated two releases ago.

At this point, you don't even want documentation.

You want to speak directly to whoever designed the feature.

Preferably over coffee.

A very long coffee.

6. The Dependencies: "I Didn't Change Anything!"

This one is particularly painful.

Your application was working yesterday.

You haven't touched the code.

You haven't changed the configuration.

You haven't even opened the project.

Today, something breaks.

You investigate.

A dependency changed.

Or two packages no longer agree about which version of a third package they need.

Or your environment resolved a different version because the dependency wasn't pinned.

Now you're debugging software you didn't write, inside an application that was already working.

And the error message somehow points to your code.

Wonderful.

Nothing makes you appreciate reproducible builds quite like a dependency problem.

7. The Previous Developer: "Who Wrote This Code?"

You're working on an existing project.

You open a function.

It's 300 lines long.

There are mysterious variable names.

Several nested conditions.

No comments.

A few hardcoded values.

And one particularly suspicious line that nobody seems willing to explain.

You look at the commit history.

You sigh.

"Who wrote this?"

Then you look at the author.

It's you.

From eight months ago.

Suddenly, you remember that the function was written during a particularly stressful deadline.

You also remember being very proud of it.

Nothing humbles a developer faster than reading their own old code.

8. The Server: "It Works on My Machine!"

Possibly the most famous sentence in software development.

Your code works locally.

The tests pass.

Everything looks beautiful.

You deploy it.

It breaks.

Naturally, your first reaction is:

"But it works on my machine."

The production environment apparently didn't get the memo.

Maybe the environment variables are different.

Maybe the file paths behave differently.

Maybe the production database contains data your local database never had.

Maybe there's a permissions issue.

Whatever the reason, the server has decided to expose the assumptions your laptop was politely hiding.

And now everyone wants to know why the deployment failed.

The server didn't necessarily break your code. It may have revealed what your code was assuming.

Not that this makes the experience any less frustrating.

9. AI: "Why Did You Give Me This Code?"

This is the newest member of the blame club.

You ask AI to write a function.

It produces beautiful code.

Proper formatting.

Meaningful names.

Helpful comments.

A confident explanation.

You run it.

Error.

You paste the error back into AI.

It apologizes and generates another version.

You run that.

Different error.

AI apologizes again.

Now you're in a debugging relationship where one of you never gets tired and the other is slowly losing patience.

Then you finally inspect the original code carefully.

The model assumed something that wasn't true.

Perhaps it invented an API method.

Perhaps it ignored a requirement.

Perhaps you didn't provide enough context.

Or perhaps the model simply made a mistake.

That's why I've increasingly preferred using AI as a reviewer and thinking partner rather than blindly accepting whatever it generates.

I explored this problem in Most Developers Test Their Code. Why Don't They Test Their AI?.

AI can generate bugs faster than we can blame it for them.

And yes, we still have to test the output.

10. Yourself: "Okay, That One Was My Fault"

Here comes the uncomfortable part.

After blaming the compiler, the internet, the cache, the framework, the documentation, the dependencies, the previous developer, the server, and AI...

You finally discover the problem.

A typo.

A missing environment variable.

An incorrect condition.

A misunderstood requirement.

Or a change you made fifteen minutes ago and somehow completely forgot about.

You stare at the screen.

Silence.

You fix the issue.

Everything works.

And now you have a very important decision to make.

Do you tell everyone what happened?

Or do you quietly close the terminal and pretend you solved a mysterious technical problem?

I believe we've all considered the second option.

At least once.

Maybe more.

The Funny Thing About Debugging

The longer I spend around technology, the more I appreciate something.

Programming isn't simply about writing code.

It's about making assumptions, testing them, discovering which ones were wrong, and correcting our understanding.

Sometimes the compiler is responsible.

Sometimes a dependency really does introduce a regression.

Sometimes the documentation genuinely is terrible.

And sometimes the problem is sitting between the keyboard and the chair.

But every frustrating bug has the potential to teach us something.

We learn to read error messages more carefully.

We learn to test our assumptions.

We learn to inspect logs before blaming infrastructure.

We learn to question AI-generated suggestions.

And hopefully, we learn to be a little kinder to the previous developer.

Especially when the previous developer was us.

One Last Confession

I think debugging has a strange relationship with our emotions.

When the code works, we feel like geniuses.

When the code breaks, we blame the technology.

When we finally identify the issue, we wonder how we missed something so obvious.

And five minutes later?

We're back to writing more code.

Because despite the frustration, there's something wonderfully satisfying about solving a problem that seemed impossible an hour ago.

Perhaps that's why we keep doing it.

Not because programming is always easy.

But because that moment when everything finally works is worth the effort.

Even if the problem was just a missing bracket.

articles.title: The Guardrails I Give My AI Coding Agent
articles.description: In my last post I wrote that the more I use AI to code, the more engineering judgment matters. A fair...
articles.body_html:
In my last post I wrote that the more I use AI to code, the more engineering judgment matters. A fair follow-up question is: what does that judgment look like on an ordinary day?

For the past few weeks, an AI coding agent (Claude Code, in my case) has been writing much of the code for our product's search pages. In one day this week it shipped four separate changes to our development environment: a new way to combine filters with a plain-text view of a search, two small visual fixes, and a layout change for smaller laptop screens.

I didn't write those changes. I did decide what got built, what shipped and what "done" meant.

Those decisions are what I want to describe. Most of them are not clever. They are guardrails: rules the agent follows every time, so that speed doesn't turn into surprises.

1. Two decisions stay with me: build it, and ship it

The agent can investigate, propose and build. When it finishes an investigation, it gives me a recommendation rather than a list of every possible option, and then it waits. My answer is usually short: "Yes, build it."

When the change is built and checked, it stops again and asks whether to ship. "Yes, ship it" is a separate decision, and it is mine.

Splitting the two matters more than it sounds. The first approval is about the idea. The second is about the result, after I have seen it. Without the second stop, approving an idea quietly turns into approving whatever came out.

2. Show me, don't tell me

A description of a UI change is not evidence. Every visual change goes onto a local preview first, and the agent sends me screenshots before anything is pushed.

Take the layout change from this week. On a smaller laptop, the panel beside our search form pushed its main buttons, View Results and Download, below the edge of the screen. The fix keeps the count at the top and the buttons at the bottom, and lets only the details between them scroll.

The agent didn't stop at "it works on my screen". It checked:

  • 1366 x 640, a common short laptop window: the buttons end 24 pixels above the bottom edge.
  • 1366 x 560, a very short window: still visible.
  • 1440 x 1000: nothing scrolls, so nothing should look different, and nothing did.
  • Tablet and phone widths, where the page uses a different layout altogether.

At each size it also ran a small script that looks for anything spilling sideways out of its container, the kind of overflow that is easy to miss at a glance.

If you take one habit from this post, take this one: decide which screen sizes count, and make "checked at those sizes, with screenshots" part of done.

3. Merge only on green, and only the commit that was tested

The agent opens a pull request and waits for CI. It merges only when every check is green, and it pins the merge to the exact commit the checks ran against:

gh pr checks "$PR" --watch --fail-fast
gh pr merge "$PR" --merge --match-head-commit "$HEAD_SHA"

--match-head-commit makes the merge fail if anything was pushed to the branch after the checks started. Without it, "CI was green" can describe a different commit from the one that lands.

A red check is never something to talk around. Either the code gets fixed, or the agent explains why the test itself is out of date, changes it in the open and says so in the pull request. It does not quietly loosen a test to get to green.

4. Tests that pin the rules people forget

Some of my favourite tests are almost embarrassingly simple. They read a source file as text and check it with a regular expression:

import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import fs from 'node:fs';

const css = fs.readFileSync('resources/css/search.css', 'utf8');

test('colours come from design tokens, never hex values', () => {
  assert.doesNotMatch(css, /#[0-9a-fA-F]{3,8}\b/);
});

A test like this caught the agent this week. To fade the edges of the new scrolling area, it used a CSS mask with #000 in the gradient. The colour never even shows (a mask only uses transparency), but the rule is the rule, and the test failed. The fix took seconds: black instead of #000. What matters is that I didn't have to notice it.

We have tests like this for:

  • no em dashes or curly quotes in customer-facing text (a single curly apostrophe in a release note failed the tests once, which is exactly what I wanted);
  • a maximum length for release note titles and summaries;
  • a line limit on one large component, which pushes new logic into its own file instead of growing one file forever.

None of these rules are hard to check. They are hard to remember, especially at the speed an agent works. A rule that lives only in a style guide will be broken eventually. A rule that lives in a test is checked every time.

5. Every change ships with its own story

Each user-facing change includes two pieces of writing in the same pull request:

  • a short "What's New" entry that customers see in the product, with a title under 70 characters and a summary under 260;
  • a line in our internal product document saying what changed, why, who asked for it and where the code lives.

The agent writes both. It knows the change better than anyone at that moment, so this is the cheapest time to write it down. Because it happens in the same pull request, the documentation never falls a release behind, and tests hold the customer-facing text to its length and style limits.

6. Check it where it lives, and leave it as you found it

Green CI and a good local preview are not the end. After each deploy, the agent opens the change on our development environment and checks it again, using my own saved search as the test case.

That comes with firm limits:

  • It never touches production.
  • It never signs in as me. If the session has expired, it tells me and waits.
  • On the development environment it reads, and avoids changing real records or running expensive exports.
  • When it has to change something to test it, such as a draft search, it saves the original first and puts it back afterwards.

The last point matters more than it seems. A test environment that slowly fills up with leftovers from automated checks stops being trustworthy.

7. Write the traps down

Every project has traps that cost an afternoon the first time. The agent keeps a notes file of them and reads it at the start of every session.

One example from our search: when the agent set up a test search using a field's internal sample name instead of its real name, the filter still appeared on screen, but the search silently ignored it. The count looked plausible and was wrong. That trap is now one line in the notes, with the rule that goes with it: always use the live field name.

The format doesn't matter much. What matters is that a lesson learned once isn't paid for again in the next session.

8. Small, boring commits

A few habits keep the history easy to read and easy to undo:

  • One change per pull request, even on a day with four of them.
  • Files are staged by name, never with a blanket git add, so scratch files and stray experiments don't ride along.
  • Commit messages say what changed for the user, not only what changed in the code.

If something goes wrong, I want to point at one small pull request and revert it without unpicking three other things.

What the guardrails are really for

None of this slows the agent down much. Most of it is automated, and the rest is two short answers from me. What it changes is what I am responsible for.

I don't need to read every line at the speed it was written. I need to be confident about the things that matter: what the change does, that it was tested at the sizes and in the situations we care about, that it follows our rules, and that what was tested is what shipped. The guardrails turn those from things I hope are true into things that are checked.

In my last post I said that if I ship something, I need to be able to explain it, debug it and maintain it. These guardrails are a large part of how I keep that promise while an agent does most of the typing.

What guardrails have you put around AI-written code? I'd especially like to hear about cheap checks that have caught real mistakes.

articles.title: I Built a Claude Code Plugin Because I Was Becoming a Rubber-Stamp Reviewer
articles.description: My development team has two members: me and AI. And lately, I've been feeling like I'm becoming the...
articles.body_html:
My development team has two members: me and AI. And lately, I've been feeling like I'm becoming the less useful member of the team.

I've been using AI coding agents for years. Claude Code, and plenty of other tools. They're incredible at what they do, but somewhere along the way, my development process started looking like this:

Me: "Implement this feature."

AI: "Done! Changed 27 files, added 3,400 lines, refactored two modules. All tests passed."

Me: "LGTM."

Narrator: He did not, in fact, look.

The code gets written. Features get shipped. Productivity looks great. But here's what bothers me: Am I actually reviewing the code anymore, or am I just approving whatever the AI tells me?

And if I'm not making the technical decisions, what exactly is my role as a developer?

The problem isn't that AI writes code

I don't think developers need to manually write every line of code. That's not the point. The problem is that we're slowly outsourcing something much more important than typing: our judgment.

Think about how often this happens. The AI makes an architectural decision without asking you. It assumes a requirement that was never specified. It changes something outside the original scope. Then it confidently reports that all tests passed, and you trust the summary because reviewing everything yourself would take too long.

None of this necessarily means the AI is bad at coding. It means our development workflow hasn't caught up with how much code AI can produce.

I wanted a workflow where AI could do most of the implementation without quietly taking ownership of the decisions. I also didn't want to become an unpaid project manager, manually breaking everything into tiny tasks and supervising every step.

So I built human-rights.


GitHub: https://github.com/kiduki77/human-rights

AI writes the code. Humans own the decisions.

human-rights is an open-source Claude Code plugin built around a simple idea: Don't make humans review every line. Make sure they understand and approve the decisions that matter.

The requirements. The architecture. The risks. The acceptance criteria. And the evidence that the implementation actually works.

But there's an obvious problem with this approach. If every tiny change requires a design document, three approvals, and a meeting with yourself, nobody is going to use it.

So the workflow adapts to the task.

  1. Not every change deserves the same process

human-rights classifies development requests into four levels, from simple edits to high-risk changes.

Level

Example

Workflow

L0 — Direct

Center a login card

Make the change and check it

L1 — Focused

Add input validation hints

Short plan and targeted tests

L2 — Planned

Add Google authentication

Investigate, design, and review

L3 — Governed

Modify safety-critical control logic

Human approvals, integration tests, and final verification

The classification considers ambiguity, scope, architectural impact, risk, verification difficulty, and dependencies. A small UI change shouldn't require the same process as modifying authentication or controlling physical hardware.

For larger changes, the agent investigates the existing code, asks questions that could change the design, and creates a testable implementation plan. If the request is too large, it first breaks the work into smaller features that can be reviewed and verified independently.

The human decides what should happen. The AI figures out how to implement it.

  1. The AI cannot simply approve its own work

This was one of the most important design decisions. I didn't want to rely entirely on instructions like "Always ask the user for approval." An AI agent following a prompt is not the same thing as an enforced workflow.

So human-rights has two parts: a Claude Code skill that decides what process a task needs, and a deterministic Python runtime that enforces state transitions, approvals, test evidence, and failure handling.

Design approvals are tied to the approved plan, while final approvals are tied to the code being verified. If the plan changes, the previous design approval becomes invalid. If the code changes, the final approval becomes invalid too.

A test result is not accepted just because the agent says it passed. The runtime records the execution result and associates it with the relevant code version.

The goal is simple: stop trusting the AI's description of what happened and start requiring evidence of what actually happened.

  1. Then I realized something worse: humans can still blindly approve everything

Even with all those safeguards, there's a fundamental weakness in the system.

The human.

You can build the most carefully controlled approval system in the world, and I can still click "Approve" without reading anything.

So I added a feature called Red Pill Mode.

Here's how it works. When enabled, the system occasionally introduces a deliberately incorrect item into the review material. The developer is supposed to notice it before approving the work.

For example, suppose the original requirement says:

The system must support four simultaneous drone connections.

But the review table contains:

TEST-010: Verify that two simultaneous drone connections work correctly.

Would you notice the difference? Or would you just approve?

If you catch the incorrect item, the system records the catch and explains why it was wrong. If you blindly approve, the approval is blocked.

And yes, it makes fun of you:

You didn't really review this, did you, human? Keep approving like that and the AI really will take your job. lol.

It's intentionally a little ridiculous, but the underlying problem is serious. An approval button means nothing if the person clicking it isn't paying attention.

The planted mistakes never modify the actual implementation plan or executable code. They exist only in the review material, so they cannot accidentally become part of the software being built.

Red Pill Mode is optional and off by default. It also supports adaptive difficulty, so the review exercises can become harder as you successfully identify mistakes.

I find this particularly interesting because we're entering a world where developers may spend more time reviewing AI-generated work than writing code themselves. If that's where we're heading, shouldn't we be actively improving our review skills instead of letting them deteriorate?

  1. Bigger requests are split before implementation

Another issue I kept encountering was asking an agent to implement something too large. It would produce an enormous plan, and I'd be expected to approve the whole thing.

That's not meaningful review. That's just outsourcing a massive amount of work and hoping the result is correct.

So compound requests are split into independently verifiable features. The human approves the feature list before implementation starts, and each feature gets its own workflow, decisions, and verification.

After those features are implemented, the system checks that they work together. Independent tasks can also run in parallel using isolated Git worktrees, while conflicting tasks are kept sequential.

The idea isn't to slow down AI development. It's to gain the speed of AI agents without giving up control of the overall design.

  1. You can try it

The project is currently at v0.5.0 and is open source under the MIT license. It runs as a Claude Code plugin with a Python 3.8+ standard-library runtime.

Install it in Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add kiduki77/human-rights

/plugin install hrs@human-rights

Initialize it in your project:

/hrs:init

Then start a task:

/hrs:new add Google authentication

Or, if you want to see whether you're actually paying attention during reviews, try:

/hrs:redpill on 5 adaptive

The repository includes an automated test suite, but this is still an early-stage project. Some integrations, including live GitHub adapter operation and real concurrent sub-agent execution, still need field validation.

GitHub: https://github.com/kiduki77/human-rights

Where this could go

Right now, human-rights focuses on individual development workflows, but I think the underlying problem could become much more important for engineering teams.

As AI generates more code, how do we know that code was meaningfully reviewed? How do we distinguish a real technical decision from a rubber-stamp approval? And how do we help developers improve at finding problems instead of gradually losing that skill?

Imagine an engineering team where AI generates most of the code. A developer approves a pull request without noticing that an important requirement was missed. Another developer catches the same issue immediately.

Today, we can track who approved a pull request, but that doesn't necessarily tell us how thoroughly it was reviewed. What if we could help developers identify the types of mistakes they tend to miss, practice reviewing realistic changes, and improve over time?

I think there's an opportunity to build something that doesn't just manage AI-generated code, but helps humans become better reviewers of it.

That's a longer-term idea, not something I'm claiming the current plugin already solves.

For now, I'm starting with the problem I experience every day: making sure I still understand and control the software I'm building.

I'd love to hear what other developers think

I'm especially curious whether other developers have noticed themselves reviewing AI-generated code less carefully over time. Would enforced approval gates help, or would they just become another form of bureaucracy? And would you actually enable something like Red Pill Mode in your own development workflow?

I don't have all the answers, and I'm sure there are things I've overlooked. That's why I'm releasing this as open source and looking for feedback from developers who are experiencing the same problems.

I built this because I don't want to stop using AI.

I just don't want to stop being a developer while using it.

human-rights — AI writes the code. Humans own the decisions.

https://github.com/kiduki77/human-rights

articles.title: rm -rf and the Sound It Makes
articles.description: The folder is empty.  Not broken. Not corrupted, not locked, not asking for a password I forgot....
articles.body_html:
The folder is empty.

Not broken. Not corrupted, not locked, not asking for a password I forgot. Empty. The name is still there on the screen, "client-portal", sitting in the list exactly where it always sat, and when I open it there is nothing inside. White space. A scrollbar that has nothing to scroll. I stare at it for a long time, the way you stare at a room after someone has moved out of it and taken everything, even the smell.

I know what I did. That is the worst part. There was no crash, no power cut, no mysterious bug to blame. I typed it. I watched it run. I pressed enter like a man posting a letter.

Three weeks of work. A client portal, the whole thing: login, dashboard, the invoice list, the file upload that took me four days because the progress bar lied and I believed it. Gone in the time it takes to blink. The command does not ask twice. It does not say "are you sure" in the tone of a friend. It just does what you told it to do, and then it waits, politely, for your next instruction, as if nothing happened.

That is the sound it makes. Nothing. No error, no warning, no sad trombone. Just the cursor, blinking, on a fresh empty line.

Forty minutes earlier I am sitting at the same desk, and the folder is full, and I am annoyed at it.

The annoyance is specific. There is a folder inside the project called "client-portal-old" and another one called "client-portal-backup", and a third one called "client-portal-final", and none of them are what their names say they are. The "final" one is from two weeks ago. The "backup" one has half the files. The "old" one is somehow newer than the "final" one. I have been meaning to clean this up for days. Today is the day. I will delete the old ones, keep the real one, and stop living like this.

I open the terminal. I type the command the way I have typed it a hundred times. The folder name after it. I check it. I check it again, because I am the kind of person who checks. The name looks right. The path looks right. I press enter.

The screen does what screens do. A line of output, gone too fast to read. And then nothing.

I do not notice at first. I notice when I look for the folder and it is not where I left it. Not the old one. The real one. The one with three weeks in it. My eyes do the thing eyes do when the brain has not caught up yet: they scan the list again, slower, as if the folder is hiding behind another folder, as if it will step out and say it was a joke.

It does not step out.

Three hours earlier, the folder is full, and I am proud of it, and that is what makes the whole thing worse.

I had just finished the file upload. Four days on a progress bar. Four days because the bar would climb to ninety percent and stop, and I would sit there watching it the way you watch a kettle, and then I found it: the thing was reporting the wrong total. It was measuring the wrong file. One line. One wrong variable, and the bar had been lying to me for a week. I fixed it in eleven minutes and sat there laughing at my own screen, alone, at my desk, because the fix was so small and the days were so long.

I showed it to a friend on a call. He watched a file climb from zero to a hundred in a straight honest line and said "nice", which is the highest praise a developer ever gives another developer. I closed the call feeling like a person who knows what he is doing. I wrote a commit message that said "upload progress fixed, finally". I meant the "finally" in the warm way. The way you say it when a thing is done.

That commit is gone too. Everything is gone. The fix, the message, the "finally". The whole three weeks, and the feeling that went with it.

The morning of the same day, the folder is full, and I am building the invoice list, and I am thinking about the name of the project.

"Client-portal" is a boring name. I know it is a boring name. I named it on the first day, in a hurry, because the folder needed a name before it needed anything else, and I never renamed it. Every project I have ever made has a boring first-day name that stuck. There is a folder on this machine called "test-final" that holds a whole website. There is one called "new-app-2" that holds the thing I am proudest of. I tell myself I will rename them one day, when there is time, and there is never time, and the names stay, and after a while the boring name starts to feel like the real name, the way a nickname you hate at first becomes the only thing anyone calls you.

I am building the invoice list and thinking about this, and about how the list needs to show the paid ones in green and the overdue ones in red, and how the red ones should not shout, just sit there quietly, because nobody likes being shouted at by an invoice. Small decisions. The kind that take ten seconds and shape the whole thing. I make about forty of them before lunch and forget thirty-nine.

A week before that, the folder is nearly empty, and I am starting.

Starting is the part nobody talks about. The first file. The blank page with a cursor on it, waiting. I sit there for twenty minutes doing nothing that looks like work: moving the window, checking the time, opening the folder and closing it again. Then I write the first line. It is a bad line. I know it is a bad line even as I write it. But it is a line, and a line is a beginning, and a beginning is the only thing a blank folder cannot give you.

By the end of the first day there are six files. By the end of the first week there are thirty. I do not remember writing most of them. I remember the stuck moments, the afternoons when nothing worked and I walked around the room and came back and it worked, and I remember the small wins, the button that finally lined up, the page that loaded in under a second. The rest is a blur, the way a road trip is a blur except for the wrong turns and the good meals.

Three weeks. Thirty-something files. One wrong command.

The folder is empty.

I sit there for a while, and then I do the only thing there is to do. I open a new folder with the same boring name, and I start again.

The second version is better. I know that sounds like the kind of thing people say to make themselves feel better, and maybe it is, but it is also true. The first version's mistakes are the one thing I remember perfectly. I remember every place I got stuck, every wrong turn, every line I wrote and then wrote around instead of fixing. This time I do not write around them. I fix them. The upload bar works on the first try. The invoice list takes an afternoon instead of two days. The login page, which took me a week the first time because I kept second-guessing it, takes a morning.

It is not faster because I am smarter. It is faster because the first version taught me where the walls are, and this time I walk around them instead of into them.

By the end of the week the folder is full again. Fuller than before, in fewer files, with fewer apologies hidden in the comments. I show it to the same friend on the same kind of call. The file climbs from zero to a hundred in a straight honest line. He says "nice". I do not tell him it is the second time he has seen it. Nobody ever knows. The client never knows. The portal ships on time, and it works, and the first version, the one with the "finally" in its commit message, never existed as far as anyone can tell.

Sometimes I open the folder just to look at it. Not to change anything. Just to see that it is full. And then I close it, and I check the path twice before I type anything, and I always will now.

The command still does not ask twice. I am the one who asks twice. Every time.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: Stop Trimming Tool Descriptions. They Were Never the Biggest Part.
articles.description: kevinhall left a comment on my piece about the 200-tool menu, and it pointed at the one split my run...
articles.body_html:
kevinhall left a comment on my piece about the 200-tool menu, and it pointed at the one split my run never made. He had measured real hosted tools, and the heaviest definition he found was almost all an output schema the server had made up from past runs, nothing the author wrote. So the cost was not always in the descriptions. My run never split the output schema out from the description and the input schema, so I could not say whether he was right, or how far it went.

I split five real server definitions open this week: the filesystem, memory, sequential-thinking, everything, and github servers, 68 tools in total, counted the same way as the earlier runs so the totals reproduce exactly. The answer is messier than either of us expected. kevinhall is right that the cost is not in the descriptions. He is wrong about where it is. And the split turned up something neither of us was looking for, hiding in the heaviest server of all.

My claim before the numbers: the output schema would be the biggest chunk on the heavy servers, and trimming descriptions would be trimming the wrong thing. The first half was wrong. The second half was right for the wrong reason.

Problem 1: the description is the biggest chunk on none of the five servers

Across all 68 tools, 23,298 tokens of definition: descriptions are 2,619 tokens, 11.2 percent. Input schemas are 6,876, 29.5 percent. Output schemas are 2,205, 9.5 percent. The description is not the largest part anywhere.

On the filesystem server, the input schema is 39.4 percent, the description 26.1, the output schema 18.1. On sequential-thinking, the input schema is 43.8 percent against a 33.8 percent description. On github, the input schema is 84.4 percent and the description is 8.0. And github has no output schema at all, on any of its 26 tools. Stripping every description on all five servers saves 2,619 tokens. The output schema alone is 2,205, nearly as big as all the descriptions put together, and the input schema is nearly three times the descriptions.

So the advice to trim descriptions is trimming the third-biggest bucket at best. It is not useless. 11 percent is 11 percent, and over forty turns it compounds. But it is not where the cost lives, and anyone selling description-trimming as the fix for definition bloat is selling a haircut for a weight problem.

Problem 2: the output schema wins on exactly one server, by 27 tokens

The memory server is the one place kevinhall's shape shows up. Its output schema is 37.3 percent, edging out its input schema at 36.4 percent, and the description is a distant third at 14.2. Stripping every description there saves 453 tokens while the output schema alone costs 1,186, two and a half times more. The three read tools, read_graph, search_nodes and open_nodes, each carry the fattest output schema in the whole set at 238 tokens: the full entity and relation shape, with per-field descriptions.

But here is the detail that changes the story. I checked the shipped server source instead of guessing, and every output schema in this set is author-written. The memory server's schemas are Zod objects written in the server's own code, reusing the same entity shape as the input schema. The filesystem server's output schema is a generic wrapper the author wrote once: {content: string}, the identical 40-token schema on fifteen of its sixteen tools, because the server returns every result as one text blob. The "everything" server's two output schemas are plain JSON Schema literals written by hand. None of them was generated from past runs. None of them describes anything the tool actually returns in particular. The filesystem one does not even try: it is a wrapper that says "the result is text", forty tokens, fifteen times over.

So kevinhall's "made up from past runs" shape does not appear on these five servers. That does not disprove his measurement. His server was a hosted one he did not name, and I could not measure it. It means the pattern is not universal. Whether an output schema dominates depends on whether the server author bothered to write one, and how rich it is. On github, the author did not bother at all. On memory, the author wrote a rich one. The cost follows the author's habits, not the protocol.

Problem 3: the heaviest server is fat with pictures

The surprise came from the heaviest server in the set. The everything test server totals 11,914 tokens across 16 tools, and 9,520 of those, 79.9 percent, are icons. Every one of its tools carries two base64-encoded SVG icons, light and dark, 595 tokens each. The single heaviest tool in the whole set, get-header-params at 898 tokens, is 595 tokens of icons, 108 of input schema, 91 of output schema, and 58 of description. The earlier run called that tool fat on schema richness. The split shows it is mostly pictures.

Strip the icons and the whole test server falls to 2,394 tokens — cheaper than the filesystem server. Whether a host even sends icons to the model is host-dependent, but they are in the listed definition, so they are in the count. And everything is a test server, so its numbers are real but not representative. It is included because it proves the point the other four servers only suggest: schema and icon richness dominates tool count. A server with 16 tools can cost more than a server with 26, because the cost was never about how many tools there are. It is about what each definition carries.

Problem 4: presence is an author choice, not a protocol fact

Step back and the pattern across all five servers is simple. 28 of 68 tools have an output schema. Github has none. The filesystem server's is a 40-token boilerplate repeated fifteen times. The memory server's is a hand-shaped entity graph. Any claim of the form "output schemas cost X percent" needs the server named alongside it, because the answer is 37 percent on one server, 18 on another, 1.4 on a third, and zero on a fourth. There is no general number. There is only the server in front of you, split open.

That is the rule I am keeping, and it is narrower than the one I went in with. Split the definition before you trim anything, because the biggest chunk is different on every server, and on most of them it is the input schema, and on one of them it is pictures. The description is never the biggest chunk. Trim it if you like. 11 percent is real money over forty turns. But trim it knowing it is the third thing on the list, not the first.

The honest limit, stated plainly: these are local stdio servers, not hosted ones. kevinhall measured a real hosted server and did not name it, so I could not re-measure his server. A hosted server that synthesises output schemas from past runs would show a much larger output-schema share than anything here. This run neither confirms nor refutes that shape. It says what the five real official servers actually carry, and what they carry is input schemas, author-written output schemas, and, on the fattest one, pictures.

Have you ever split one of your own tool definitions open? I would like to hear what the fattest part turned out to be, and whether it was the part you expected.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: TypeScript `Const` Assertions on Function Arguments in 2026: When Inline `as const` Beats a Generic Constraint
articles.description: Inline as const on function arguments preserves literal types without generic constraints. Learn when to apply const assertions at the call site versus encoding them in the function signature.
articles.body_html:
TypeScript Const Assertions on Function Arguments in 2026: When Inline as const Beats a Generic Constraint

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Developers preserve literal types by adding generic constraints to function signatures. This forces every caller to satisfy the constraint, even when the function does not need narrower types. The function signature grows complex, and callers lose flexibility. When a route definition function demands a constraint like T extends readonly string[], teams must decide whether that constraint belongs in the signature or at the call site.

TypeScript 3.4 introduced const assertions with as const syntax (documented in the TypeScript 3.4 release notes), allowing developers to freeze literal types at the expression level. When applied inline to function arguments, as const narrows the type at the call site without changing the function signature. The function accepts the widened type, but the caller supplies a narrowed literal that TypeScript preserves through inference.

This pattern shifts type narrowing from the function's responsibility to the caller's control. The function signature stays simple. Callers who need narrow types add as const. Callers who prefer flexibility omit it. Teams avoid encoding every type requirement in the function signature itself.

Key Takeaways

  • Inline as const on function arguments preserves literal types without changing the function signature, shifting narrowing control from function author to caller.
  • Generic constraints like T extends readonly string[] force every caller to satisfy the constraint even when the function logic works with widened types.
  • Applying as const at the call site allows the function to accept both wide and narrow types, with callers choosing which behavior they need.
  • Combining const type parameters (<const T> syntax in TypeScript 5.0+) with inline assertions provides granular control over which arguments narrow and which stay flexible.
  • Inline as const breaks type inference when the compiler cannot unify the narrowed type with the function's expected parameter type, requiring explicit type annotations to resolve.

Why Generic Constraints Fall Short for Literal Preservation

Generic constraints enforce type boundaries but do not preserve literal specificity. A constraint like T extends string accepts both "GET" and string, yet the function's return type sees only the constraint's upper bound. The literal information vanishes.

function defineRoute<T extends string>(method: T) {
  return { method };
}

const route = defineRoute("GET");
// route.method has type string, not "GET"

The constraint ensures method is a string, but TypeScript widens "GET" to string during inference. The returned object loses the literal type. Discriminated unions, exhaustiveness checks, and autocomplete all depend on literal preservation. When the type widens, these features break.

Adding readonly to the constraint does not solve this. A constraint like T extends readonly string[] still widens individual elements to string. The array becomes immutable, but the element types lose their literals. Teams often add both a constraint and a manual type assertion in the function body, creating redundant type logic.

The TypeScript 3.4 release notes document const assertions as freezing literal types on simple expressions. Applying as const to an object literal makes all properties readonly and preserves each value's literal type. When applied to an array, the result becomes a readonly tuple with literal element types. This behavior extends to function arguments when the assertion appears at the call site.

Inline as const on Function Arguments: Syntax and Mechanics

Placing as const on a function argument applies the assertion before the function receives the value. The caller freezes the type, and the function sees the narrowed result. The function signature itself does not change.

function registerHandler(event: string, callback: () => void) {
  // implementation
}

registerHandler("click" as const, () => {});

The event parameter accepts string, but the caller supplies "click" narrowed to its literal type. TypeScript infers the argument as "click", not string. If the function's implementation uses event in a discriminated union or passes it to another function expecting literals, the narrow type propagates.

This syntax works with objects, arrays, and tuples:

function processConfig(config: { mode: string; flags: string[] }) {
  // implementation
}

processConfig({
  mode: "production",
  flags: ["optimize", "minify"]
} as const);

The config parameter accepts an object with string and string[] properties. The caller passes an object with mode: "production" and flags: readonly ["optimize", "minify"]. TypeScript preserves these literal types. The function signature did not require readonly or literal constraints, yet the caller achieves the same narrowing.

TypeScript const assertion syntax comparison

The TypeScript 3.4 release notes state that const assertions apply only to simple literal expressions. Attempting to assert a computed value or conditional expression fails at compile time. The assertion must wrap the literal directly.

Developers gain flexibility by choosing where to apply as const. A function accepting configuration objects can serve callers who need strict literals and callers who prefer dynamic values. The function author writes one signature. Callers who need narrow types add the assertion. Callers who do not need it omit the assertion and pass regular values.

Real-World Scenarios: Route Configs, Event Maps, and Discriminated Unions

Route configuration functions demonstrate the pattern's value. A routing library accepts an array of route definitions. Each route has a method, path, and handler. The library's internal logic dispatches based on exact method strings like "GET" or "POST". If the method type widens to string, the dispatcher cannot narrow the union correctly.

function defineRoutes(routes: Array<{
  method: string;
  path: string;
  handler: () => void;
}>) {
  return routes;
}

const routes = defineRoutes([
  { method: "GET", path: "/users", handler: () => {} },
  { method: "POST", path: "/users", handler: () => {} }
] as const);

// routes[0].method has type "GET", not string

The function signature accepts string for method, but the caller applies as const to the array. Each route's method preserves its literal type. The dispatcher can now narrow based on route.method === "GET" without type guards.

Event maps follow the same pattern. A framework's event emitter accepts an object mapping event names to payload types. The emitter's on method uses the map to enforce that listeners receive the correct payload. If event names widen to string, the map's keys lose their discriminating power.

function createEmitter<T extends Record<string, unknown>>(events: T) {
  return {
    on<K extends keyof T>(event: K, listener: (data: T[K]) => void) {
      // implementation
    }
  };
}

const emitter = createEmitter({
  click: { x: 0, y: 0 },
  keypress: { key: "" }
} as const);

emitter.on("click", (data) => {
  // data has type { readonly x: 0; readonly y: 0 }
});

The events parameter accepts any object, but the caller applies as const. Each event name becomes a literal, and each payload preserves its exact shape. The on method's listener receives a narrowed data parameter based on the event key.

Discriminated unions in state machines rely on literal types to distinguish variants. A state reducer accepts an action with a type field. The reducer switches on action.type to handle each case. If type widens to string, the switch statement loses exhaustiveness checking.

function reducer(state: State, action: { type: string; payload?: unknown }) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "increment":
      return { ...state, count: state.count + 1 };
    case "decrement":
      return { ...state, count: state.count - 1 };
    default:
      return state;
  }
}

reducer(state, { type: "increment" } as const);

The action parameter accepts type: string, but the caller supplies type: "increment" with as const. The reducer's switch statement sees the literal type and narrows accordingly. TypeScript detects when a case is missing.

These scenarios share a common need: the function logic operates on wide types, but downstream code requires narrow literals. Encoding the narrowness in the function signature forces every caller to satisfy it. Applying as const at the call site shifts the responsibility to callers who need it.

Generic Constraints vs Inline as const: When Each One Wins

Generic constraints enforce invariants across all callers. When every invocation must satisfy a type requirement, the constraint belongs in the signature. Inline as const grants flexibility. When some callers need narrow types and others do not, the assertion belongs at the call site.

Aspect Generic Constraint Inline as const
Enforcement Mandatory for all callers Optional per call site
Signature complexity Adds type parameters and bounds No signature change
Type narrowing Preserves constraint bound only Preserves exact literals
Flexibility Uniform behavior Caller-controlled behavior
Use case Invariants required by function logic Narrowing needed by caller logic

A validation function that checks an array's contents requires a constraint. The function's implementation depends on the array being readonly to avoid mutation during validation. Every caller must pass a readonly array. The constraint enforces this.

function validate<T extends readonly unknown[]>(values: T) {
  // implementation depends on immutability
}

The constraint communicates to callers that mutation is forbidden. Attempting to pass a mutable array fails at compile time. This is a true invariant of the function's contract.

A formatting function that accepts a string does not require a constraint. The function's implementation works with any string, but some callers need to preserve the specific string literal for autocomplete or discriminated unions elsewhere. Those callers add as const.

function formatMessage(template: string) {
  return template.replace(/%s/g, "value");
}

formatMessage("User %s logged in" as const);

Generic constraints versus inline assertions comparison

The function signature accepts string because the implementation does not care about narrowness. Callers who need the literal type for other purposes add the assertion. Callers who do not need it pass a plain string.

Teams evaluate whether the narrowness benefits the function's implementation or the caller's context. If the function's logic requires it, use a constraint. If the caller's downstream code requires it, use as const at the call site. When both need it, combine them.

Combining Both: Const Type Parameters and Inline Assertions

TypeScript 5.0 introduced const type parameters with the syntax <const T>. This signals that the type parameter should infer as narrow as possible without requiring as const at the call site. The function signature requests narrow inference, but callers retain the option to override it.

function createConfig<const T>(values: T) {
  return values;
}

const config = createConfig({ mode: "production", flags: ["optimize"] });
// config has type { readonly mode: "production"; readonly flags: readonly ["optimize"] }

The <const T> parameter tells TypeScript to infer T with literal types. The caller passes a plain object without as const, yet the result preserves literals. This reverses the control: the function author requests narrow inference, and callers must opt out by explicitly widening the type.

Combining <const T> with inline as const provides granular control. A function accepting multiple parameters can request narrow inference for one parameter and allow wide inference for another. Callers apply as const to specific arguments as needed.

function defineAction<const T>(type: T, payload: unknown) {
  return { type, payload };
}

const action = defineAction("increment", { amount: 5 } as const);
// action.type has type "increment"
// action.payload has type { readonly amount: 5 }

The type parameter uses <const T> to infer narrowly. The payload parameter accepts unknown, and the caller applies as const to narrow its shape. The function signature remains concise. Callers control which parts narrow.

This combination suits APIs where some arguments always need literals and others sometimes do. A router's path parameter always needs a literal string for type-safe route matching. The handler parameter might accept a plain function or a narrowed configuration object depending on the route's needs.

function route<const P>(path: P, handler: () => void) {
  return { path, handler };
}

route("/users/:id", () => {});
// path has type "/users/:id"

The <const P> parameter ensures path always infers as a literal. Callers do not need to remember to add as const. The handler parameter stays flexible. When a caller needs to narrow the handler's configuration, they apply as const to that argument only.

Developers apply this pattern selectively. Requesting narrow inference for every parameter makes the signature rigid. Applying it to parameters where narrowness benefits the function's type safety (like path patterns or discriminated union tags) keeps the API intuitive. Callers supply as const for additional narrowing when their specific use case demands it.

Common Pitfalls: When Inline as const Breaks Inference

TypeScript's type inference engine attempts to unify the narrowed type with the function's expected parameter type. When the narrowed type contains properties or shapes the parameter type does not expect, inference fails. The compiler reports that the types are incompatible.

function processData(data: { value: number }) {
  // implementation
}

processData({ value: 42, extra: "field" } as const);
// Error: Object literal may only specify known properties

The data parameter expects an object with a value property of type number. The caller supplies an object with an additional extra property and applies as const. TypeScript narrows the object to { readonly value: 42; readonly extra: "field" }. This type does not match { value: number } because of the excess property. The function signature must explicitly allow excess properties or the caller must omit them.

Applying as const to computed values fails because the TypeScript 3.4 release notes restrict const assertions to simple literal expressions. Attempting to assert a function call or conditional expression produces a compile error.

const value = (Math.random() < 0.5 ? "a" : "b") as const;
// Error: A 'const' assertion can only be applied to a string, number, boolean, array, or object literal

The assertion must wrap the literal directly. Developers who need to narrow a computed value must assign it to a const variable first, then reference that variable. The variable declaration applies the assertion implicitly.

const value = Math.random() < 0.5 ? ("a" as const) : ("b" as const);

This syntax asserts each branch of the conditional separately. The resulting type is the union "a" | "b", which preserves both literals.

Deep nesting in object literals causes TypeScript's inference to slow down when as const applies. Large configuration objects with many nested levels can trigger performance warnings. The compiler must traverse the entire structure to apply readonly and preserve literals at every level. Teams break large objects into smaller const variables to avoid this.

const baseConfig = { mode: "production" } as const;
const flags = ["optimize", "minify"] as const;

const config = { ...baseConfig, flags };

Spreading const variables composes the final object without requiring a single assertion on a deeply nested structure. Each variable narrows independently, and the spread combines them. This approach scales better than applying as const to a massive literal.

Readonly properties in const-asserted objects prevent mutation but do not prevent reassignment of the object itself. A const-asserted array becomes a readonly tuple, but the variable holding that array can still be reassigned unless declared with const.

let routes = [{ method: "GET" }] as const;
routes = [{ method: "POST" }] as const; // allowed

The routes variable is mutable. The array itself is readonly, meaning you cannot push or modify elements, but reassigning the entire variable succeeds. Developers who need true immutability declare the variable with const in addition to applying as const to the value.

Understanding these pitfalls helps teams apply inline as const correctly. The pattern works when the narrowed type remains compatible with the function's parameter type, when the assertion applies to a simple literal, and when performance remains acceptable. When these conditions hold, inline as const provides type narrowing without signature complexity.

Frequently Asked Questions

When should a function signature use a generic constraint instead of expecting callers to apply as const?

When the function's implementation depends on a type property that every caller must satisfy, encode it as a generic constraint. A validation function that iterates over a readonly array needs the constraint T extends readonly unknown[] because mutation during iteration breaks the logic. When the function works with both wide and narrow types and only some callers need narrowness, omit the constraint and let callers apply as const as needed.

Does applying as const to a function argument change the runtime behavior?

No. Const assertions are a compile-time type annotation. The TypeScript 3.4 release notes clarify that as const signals to the compiler that literal types should not widen. The compiled JavaScript code is identical to code without the assertion. The difference is purely in the type information TypeScript tracks.

Can inline as const preserve literal types through multiple function calls?

Yes, as long as each function in the chain preserves the type. If the first function returns the narrowed value and the second function accepts it without widening, the literals propagate. Breaking the chain happens when an intermediate function's return type widens the value. Generic type parameters that preserve the input type (like <T>(value: T) => T) maintain the chain.

What is the difference between const type parameters in TypeScript 5.0 and inline as const?

Const type parameters (<const T>) request narrow inference at the function signature level, applying to all callers by default. Inline as const applies at the call site, giving each caller control over whether to narrow. Combining both allows the function to request narrow inference for specific parameters while letting callers selectively narrow others with inline assertions.

Does as const work with rest parameters or variadic tuple types?

Yes. Applying as const to an array passed as a rest parameter narrows it to a readonly tuple. The function signature must accept the tuple type, either through a generic constraint or by declaring the rest parameter with readonly. When the function expects ...args: unknown[], passing ...[1, 2, 3] as const preserves the tuple type readonly [1, 2, 3].

Choosing the Right Pattern for 2026

Inline as const on function arguments shifts type narrowing control from the function signature to the call site. Function authors write simpler signatures that accept wide types. Callers who need literal preservation add the assertion. Callers who prefer flexibility omit it. This pattern reduces signature complexity while maintaining type safety for callers who need it.

Generic constraints still enforce invariants when every caller must satisfy a type requirement. Combining const type parameters with inline assertions provides granular control, allowing function authors to request narrow inference for some parameters while leaving others flexible. Teams evaluate whether narrowness benefits the function's logic or the caller's downstream code, then apply the appropriate pattern. When the function's implementation requires narrow types, use a constraint. When only some callers need them, use inline as const at the call site.

Understanding when inference breaks (excess properties, computed values, deep nesting) prevents runtime surprises and keeps compile times manageable. As TypeScript's inference engine evolves, inline as const remains a low-overhead pattern for preserving literal types without encoding every requirement in the function signature.

articles.body_html:
I'm not an expert. I'm 53, I work in a warehouse during the day, and at night I build small JavaScript projects: a 2D game engine, a debugging HUD called BeeLadybug, and a little HTML5 games portal.

They are small projects. But I care about them a lot.

My little method: docs = bug hunting

I found a method that works for me. I write the documentation of my own projects, and I publish it on my site.

While I write, I read the code. Then I read it again. And again. When I have to explain a module in plain words, I suddenly see the strange parts: a method that does too much, a default that makes no sense, a case nobody tested.

So the docs and the bug fixing grow together. Every page I write is also a small code review.

Where AI helps me

I'll be honest: I use AI a lot. It helps me understand code, write prompts for my editor, fix bugs, and polish my English (yes, this post too).

Without it, I would be much slower. I'm grateful for that.

Where AI goes wrong with me

But there is one thing that makes me crazy.

For months I have explained to different AI assistants that my projects are open source. They are on GitHub. I publish them on npm. They are made for other developers, not for me.

And still, again and again, the answer starts from the idea that these are "personal" projects. Little toys for myself.

Why? I think the reasoning is something like: one person, no team, no company, no millions… so it must be a hobby for himself.

That hurts a bit. Being alone doesn't mean building alone for myself.

A real example: the CanvasAdapter and the DOM

Tonight I was testing the Chrome extension version of BeeLadybug.

  • On normal websites, the DOM and CSS part works great. On a real games site it found a distorted image, a slider overflowing the viewport and a trapped z-index. Real bugs, on a site that is not mine.
  • On canvas games, the HUD said: CanvasAdapter attached (0 entities). A canvas is just pixels. The browser doesn't know where the player or the enemy is, only the game knows. So from outside, the extension can't draw hitboxes unless the game shares its entities.
  • And I found a real bug: BeeLadybug draws its overlays on its own <canvas> elements. If a page has a rule like canvas { background: green; }, my transparent overlay becomes a green wall that covers the game.

That bug only appears on other people's pages, with other people's CSS. If BeeLadybug were just for me, I would never have found it. That is exactly why "it's open source, for others" matters.

So… trust AI or not?

My answer today:

  • Trust it to explain, to suggest, to speed you up.
  • Don't trust it blindly. Test everything yourself. Read the code again. Ask "why?".
  • Correct it when it makes wrong assumptions about you and your work. Again and again, if needed.

AI doesn't know your story. You do.

My projects are small, and maybe my code is not perfect. But they are public, they are free, and they are made for you.

If you want to try BeeLadybug and break it on your own site, I'd love that. That's how it gets better. 🐞💚

articles.description: Our pricing service is a Node.js application that holds the current trade price of every product we...
articles.body_html:
Our pricing service is a Node.js application that holds the current trade price of every product we sell. Suppliers send new price lists with an effective date, and when a list is loaded the service sets a timer for that moment: setTimeout(activate, effectiveAt minus now). When the timer fires, the new prices replace the old. On startup the service reads pending lists from the database and sets their timers again, so a restart loses nothing.

On the third of October our largest timber supplier sent their winter prices, nine percent higher, effective on the first of November. They were live on the third of October, a few seconds after the file was loaded. For nine days our branches charged November prices, until a trade customer compared two invoices and asked why the price had gone up a month before the supplier's letter said it would.

The timer's delay is stored as a signed 32 bit integer of milliseconds. The largest value it can hold is 2,147,483,647, a little under twenty four days and twenty one hours. Node's documentation says what happens to anything bigger: the delay is set to one millisecond. Node prints a TimeoutOverflowWarning when it does, and ours went into the logs between two lines about the price file's size. Twenty nine days is about 2.5 billion milliseconds, so the timer fired as soon as it could.

It had worked for four years because suppliers had always given us two or three weeks' notice. This one gave four. Nothing in our code was new. The input had crossed a limit the code had always had.

We refunded the difference to every account that had paid it, which took finance most of a week. The pricing service no longer schedules anything far in advance. A job runs every minute and activates any price list whose effective time has passed, reading the time from the database, so a list due in a year and a list due in a minute go through the same code. Where we still use timers, for retries and timeouts, a helper refuses any delay over a day. And our tests now load a price list effective in ninety days and check that the old prices are still in force afterwards.

A timer has a range like any other number. Ours was twenty four days, and our suppliers finally gave us more notice than that.

– Sergey Shinder
